chunks.heading: The Universe Switches On
chunks.text: 01 13.8 billion years ago The Universe Switches On Every atom in your body has a very, very long backstory. Strong. 13.8 billion years ago The Universe Switches On Every atom in your body has a very, very long backstory. Strong You are there Stand on the young Earth about 4.4 billion years ago and the ground is brand new. Tiny zircon crystals that will one day turn up in the Jack Hills of Western Australia are forming right now, and their chemistry hints that liquid water already pools at the surface. The Sun overhead is fainter than today's, perhaps 70 percent as bright, yet the planet is not frozen solid, a puzzle scientists still argue about. Rocks from space crash down far more often than they ever will again. The Moon, most likely born when a planet-sized body slammed into the growing Earth, hangs much closer than it does now; it has been drifting away ever since and still retreats about 3.8 centimetres a year. There is no life anyone can point to yet, no oxygen to breathe, and nobody to watch. But the ingredients are here: water, rock, energy, and carbon and oxygen cooked inside stars that lived and died before the Sun was born. The numbers Age of the universe 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years Measured from the pattern of the cosmic microwave background, the afterglow of the hot early universe. Planck Collaboration 2020, Astronomy & Astrophysics NEW Earliest confirmed galaxy ~300 million years after the Big Bang JWST spectra confirmed JADES-GS-z14-0 at redshift 14.32, showing bright galaxies formed surprisingly early. Carniani et al. 2024, Nature Solar System's first solids 4.567 billion years ago Calcium-aluminium-rich grains in meteorites are the oldest dated objects formed in our Solar System. Connelly et al. 2012, Science Age of Earth 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years Base

chunks.heading: From Slime to Dinosaurs
chunks.text: 02 4.2 billion to 66 million years ago From Slime to Dinosaurs For most of Earth's history the planet belonged to microbes, and they did a lot of the heavy lifting. Strong. 4.2 billion to 66 million years ago From Slime to Dinosaurs For most of Earth's history the planet belonged to microbes, and they did a lot of the heavy lifting. Strong You are there It is about 508 million years ago and you are drifting over a muddy sea floor at the foot of an underwater cliff, in rocks that will one day be lifted into the Canadian Rockies. The water is busy. Trilobites plough through the mud on jointed legs. Opabinia swims past with five stalked eyes and a long flexible nozzle tipped with a grasping claw. Hallucigenia, a spiny, worm-like creature so strange that scientists first drew it upside down and back to front, picks its way across a sponge. Anomalocaris, a predator with spiny grasping limbs in front of its mouth, cruises overhead. On land there is almost nothing to see: no forests, no flowers, nothing walking on the dry ground beyond crusts of microbes. Oxygen has been building up in the air for nearly two billion years, thanks to microbes that learned to split water using sunlight. Now animals with eyes, shells and appetites are trying out every way to build a body. Soon a flow of mud will bury this scene and preserve it in astonishing detail. The numbers NEW Last universal common ancestor (LUCA) ~4.2 billion years ago A molecular-clock study estimates LUCA lived about 4.09–4.33 billion years ago and was already a fairly complex cell. Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution Oldest widely accepted fossil reef ~3.43 billion years Layered stromatolites built by microbial mats in the Strelley Pool Formation, Western Australia. Allwood et al. 2006, Nature Great Oxidation E

chunks.heading: Getting Up on Two Feet
chunks.text: 03 7 million to 400,000 years ago Getting Up on Two Feet Before big brains, fire or spears, our ancestors made one bold move: they stood up. Hot debate. 7 million to 400,000 years ago Getting Up on Two Feet Before big brains, fire or spears, our ancestors made one bold move: they stood up. Hot debate You are there About 3.66 million years ago, on the plains of what is now northern Tanzania, the volcano Sadiman has been puffing out fine ash. A light shower turns the grey powder into something like wet cement, and raindrops leave little craters in it. Every creature that crosses leaves a record. Hares hop through. Three-toed horses clip past. Guineafowl scratch about. Then come upright walkers, small by our standards, probably members of Australopithecus afarensis, the species of the famous Lucy skeleton. Their feet have an arch and a big toe in line with the others, much like yours, and their stride looks surprisingly human. Some prints are small; tracks found nearby in 2015 suggest one individual stood around 1.65 metres tall. Nobody carries a spear or wears clothes. They are simply going somewhere, across a landscape shared with grazing animals. The sun bakes the ash hard, more ash falls on top, and the walk is sealed away until Mary Leakey's team uncovers it in 1978. The numbers Human-chimp split ~7–8 million years ago Genetic mutation-rate estimates place the divergence of our lineage from chimpanzees' in this window. Langergraber et al. 2012, PNAS Lucy 3.18 million years old About 40 percent of one Australopithecus afarensis skeleton, found in Ethiopia in 1974. Johanson & Taieb 1976, Nature Laetoli footprints 3.66 million years old The main trail runs for about 27 metres through volcanic ash. Leakey & Hay 1979, Nature Oldest known stone tools 3.3 million years Lomek

chunks.heading: Meet the Cousins
chunks.text: 04 1 million to 40,000 years ago Meet the Cousins For most of our story we were not alone: the world was full of other kinds of humans. Hot debate. 1 million to 40,000 years ago Meet the Cousins For most of our story we were not alone: the world was full of other kinds of humans. Hot debate You are there In a limestone cave above the Anui River in Siberia's Altai Mountains, roughly 90,000 years ago, a girl of at least 13 is living her short life. No one will ever know her name; scientists will call her Denisova 11, or Denny. Her mother is a Neanderthal whose ancestors were more closely related to Neanderthals living far to the west, in Europe. Her father is a Denisovan, a member of a population so poorly known that most of what we know about it comes from DNA pulled out of bone crumbs and teeth. Her father himself carries a little Neanderthal ancestry from further back. The cave has been used on and off by both groups for a very long time. Of Denny herself, only a sliver of long bone about 2 centimetres long survives, sorted as an unremarkable scrap among thousands until a protein screen flagged it as human. Her genome is the first direct genetic evidence of a child whose parents came from two different kinds of humans. The numbers Neanderthals disappear ~41,000–39,000 years ago Radiocarbon dating across Europe suggests Neanderthal sites end in this window, with overlap with modern humans. Higham et al. 2014, Nature Denisovans discovered 2010 First identified from the genome of a finger bone, before anyone knew what they looked like. Reich et al. 2010, Nature NEW Harbin 'Dragon Man' identified at least 146,000 years old Ancient proteins and mitochondrial DNA from dental calculus link this near-complete skull to Denisovans. Fu et al. 2025, Science; Fu et al. 2025, Cell N

chunks.heading: Enter Homo sapiens
chunks.text: 05 ~315,000 to 45,000 years ago Enter Homo sapiens Our species starts out in Africa, then spreads everywhere, flirting with the cousins along the way. Hot debate. ~315,000 to 45,000 years ago Enter Homo sapiens Our species starts out in Africa, then spreads everywhere, flirting with the cousins along the way. Hot debate You are there On Muna, a small island off southeast Sulawesi, someone steps into the cave now called Liang Metanduno at least 67,800 years ago. They press a hand flat against the limestone wall and blow a spray of red pigment around it, probably by mouth. Then they do something clever: they adjust the outline so the fingertips look narrow and pointed, almost like claws. When the hand lifts away, a ghostly red silhouette remains. What did it mean? A signature, a ritual, a joke between friends? Nobody can say. Over tens of thousands of years, thin mineral crusts grow over the paint, and in the 2020s scientists date those crusts with uranium-series methods, which gives a minimum age for the art beneath. The artist was probably one of our own species, perhaps among the people whose relatives went on to reach Australia, though the researchers admit they cannot fully rule out another kind of human. Either way, it is one of the oldest known marks of imagination still on a cave wall. The numbers Oldest Homo sapiens-like fossils 315,000 ± 34,000 years Skulls and teeth from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, with a modern-looking face but a longer braincase. Richter et al. 2017, Nature Omo Kibish I at least 233,000 years old Dating of volcanic ash places this Ethiopian skull among the oldest of our species. Vidal et al. 2022, Nature NEW Main Neanderthal mixing ~50,500–43,500 years ago Averaged around 47,000 years ago and lasting roughly 7,000 years. Iasi et al. 2024, Science

chunks.heading: Life in the Big Freeze
chunks.text: 06 ~26,500 to 14,700 years ago Life in the Big Freeze Sea levels dropped, land bridges opened, and people walked into places no human had ever seen. Strong. ~26,500 to 14,700 years ago Life in the Big Freeze Sea levels dropped, land bridges opened, and people walked into places no human had ever seen. Strong You are there It is about 22,000 years ago in what is now New Mexico. Ice sheets bury most of Canada, but here in the Tularosa Basin a shallow lake spreads across the valley floor, fringed by soft, damp mud. A group of people splash along the edge. Many of the footprints they leave are small: teenagers and children, some tracks crossing and recrossing as if they were playing or running errands. The same basin's mud also holds tracks of mammoths and giant ground sloths, animals that still roam North America. Seeds of a water plant called ditchgrass sink into the shallows, and pollen from conifers drifts down from the hills. Thousands of years later, those seeds, that pollen, grains of quartz and ancient lake mud will each be dated by independent teams and methods, and they keep landing between roughly 21,000 and 23,000 years ago. If those dates hold, these kids were walking in the Americas thousands of years before most textbooks said anyone had arrived. The numbers Last Glacial Maximum ~26,500–19,000 years ago The interval when ice sheets were at their largest. Clark et al. 2009, Science Sea level at the peak ~125–135 m lower So much water was locked in ice that continental shelves became dry land. chunks.heading: The Great Melt
chunks.text: 07 14,700 to 8,000 years ago The Great Melt The ice cracked, the seas rose, and the climate lurched like a car with a learner driver. No receipts yet. 14,700 to 8,000 years ago The Great Melt The ice cracked, the seas rose, and the climate lurched like a car with a learner driver. No receipts yet You are there Somewhere on the coast of what is now South Australia, generation after generation, the sea is coming closer. As the world's great ice sheets melt, ocean levels climb: on average about a metre a century, and faster during meltwater pulses. Grandparents point to places where they once walked dry-footed that are now under water. Hunting grounds turn into shallows, then open sea. Hills become islands. People adjust: they move camps, rename places, and above all they tell each other what happened. Thousands of years later, Aboriginal stories recorded by outsiders in the 19th and 20th centuries describe a time when the coastline lay far out, when islands were joined to the mainland, and when the sea rose and drowned the land. Geographer Patrick Nunn and linguist Nicholas Reid argue that some of these stories may preserve real memories of shorelines that vanished more than 7,000 years ago. If they are right, these are among the oldest surviving accounts passed down by word of mouth anywhere on Earth. The numbers Bølling warming ~9 °C in decades Around 14,700 years ago Greenland warmed abruptly by about 9 ± 3 °C. chunks.heading: Monuments Before Farms
chunks.text: 08 ~11,600 to 10,000 years ago Monuments Before Farms People carved giant stone pillars before they had fully become farmers, which flipped an old textbook story on its head. Hot debate. ~11,600 to 10,000 years ago Monuments Before Farms People carved giant stone pillars before they had fully become farmers, which flipped an old textbook story on its head. Hot debate You are there On a limestone ridge above the Harran plain in what is now southeastern Türkiye, around 11,000 years ago, people are cutting a pillar out of the bedrock. They have no metal tools and no domesticated animals to haul loads, only stone, rope, wood and muscle. When a T-shaped pillar is finished, carvers bring it to life with foxes, boars, snakes, cranes and vultures. On some pillars, arms and hands wrap around the sides above a belt and a fox-pelt loincloth, as if the stone were a stylised person. Nearby, grinding slabs turn wild cereals into mash or dough. Bones of wild gazelle and aurochs pile up, perhaps from large gatherings. Out in the quarry, an unfinished pillar about 7 metres long still lies in the rock, abandoned, possibly after it cracked. Nobody here is a farmer in the full sense yet. That is exactly why archaeologists are still arguing about what this place was for. The numbers Göbekli Tepe begins ~9500 BCE Radiocarbon dates put the large pillar enclosures in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, about 11,500 years ago. Dietrich et al. 2012, Antiquity Biggest pillars up to ~5.5 m tall Central pillars in the largest enclosures may weigh around 10 tonnes. chunks.heading: Farming Changes Everything
chunks.text: 09 ~12,000 to 8,000 years ago Farming Changes Everything Humans tamed wheat, rice, maize, goats and cattle, and in return, farming tamed us. Hot debate. ~12,000 to 8,000 years ago Farming Changes Everything Humans tamed wheat, rice, maize, goats and cattle, and in return, farming tamed us. Hot debate You are there It is around 7000 BCE on the Konya Plain in central Anatolia, and there are no streets. Çatalhöyük is a honeycomb of mud-brick houses packed wall to wall, and you get home by walking across the rooftops and climbing down a ladder through a hole that also lets the smoke from the oven out. Inside, the walls are plastered white and sometimes painted; horns of wild cattle are set into benches and walls. Some of the dead lie beneath the platforms where the living sleep. Families grow wheat, barley, peas and lentils, herd sheep and goats, and still hunt wild animals. Ancient DNA from more than a hundred people buried here hints at a surprise: relatives buried beneath the same houses were often linked through their mothers' lines, and females tended to receive more grave goods. Life is crowded and busy, and in some ways harder than foraging; skeletons show rising tooth decay and head injuries. Still, people keep living here for well over a thousand years. The numbers Independent farming inventions at least 11 regions Plants and animals were domesticated separately in places including the Fertile Crescent, China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica and the Andes. Larson et al. 2014, PNAS Domesticated wheat and barley by ~10,500 years ago Domestication in the Fertile Crescent was a slow process spread over centuries to millennia. chunks.heading: Cities and the First Writing
chunks.text: 10 ~5,500 to 3,900 years ago Cities and the First Writing Writing was not invented for poetry. It was invented because somebody needed to count the barley. No receipts yet. ~5,500 to 3,900 years ago Cities and the First Writing Writing was not invented for poetry. It was invented because somebody needed to count the barley. No receipts yet You are there Uruk, southern Mesopotamia, around 3200 BCE. The city is enormous for its time, with perhaps tens of thousands of people, temple precincts decorated with mosaics of coloured clay cones, and canals branching off from the Euphrates. In a storeroom, an administrator wets a lump of clay, flattens it into a tablet and presses a reed stylus into it: a sign for barley, round and crescent-shaped marks for quantities, a sign group that might be a person's name or a job title. This is not literature. Most of the earliest tablets are bookkeeping: rations, livestock, workers, beer. One often-quoted tablet tallies barley over 37 months and carries a sign group read as Kushim, which might be the earliest recorded name of a person, or might simply be an office. Nobody here thinks they are inventing history. They are trying not to lose track of the grain. Within a few centuries, scribes will be writing hymns, laws and stories. The numbers Earliest cuneiform tablets ~3300–3100 BCE About 85 percent of the proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk are administrative records; most of the rest are word lists. Englund 1998, Texts from the Late Uruk Period Earliest Egyptian writing ~3250 BCE Small bone and ivory labels from tomb U-j at Abydos carry some of the first hieroglyphic signs. Dreyer 1998, Umm el-Qaab I Writing invented at least 3 times Independently in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably also in Egypt. Woods (ed.) 2010, Visible

chunks.heading: The Age of Pyramids
chunks.text: 11 ~4,700 to 4,000 years ago The Age of Pyramids Giant tombs, giant stones hauled across Britain, and a drought that may or may not have toppled kings. Hot debate. ~4,700 to 4,000 years ago The Age of Pyramids Giant tombs, giant stones hauled across Britain, and a drought that may or may not have toppled kings. Hot debate You are there Around 2560 BCE, an inspector named Merer is keeping a logbook on papyrus. He leads a team of roughly 40 men, and they work the Nile by boat. Their job: collect blocks of fine white limestone at the quarries of Tura, across the river, and ferry them to Giza, where King Khufu's pyramid is rising. The diary notes, day by day, where the crew sleeps and when they sail, and it mentions a basin called the Lake of Khufu near the building site, reachable by boat when the water is high. Merer's crew are not the whip-driven masses of old films; they are organised, supplied and recorded, part of a state machine able to move millions of tonnes of stone. About 4,500 years later, in 2013, fragments of Merer's diary turn up at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast, a harbour where his team later worked. They are the oldest inscribed papyri yet found, and they give us the building of the Great Pyramid in the words of someone who was there. The numbers Great Pyramid 146.6 m (original height) Built for Khufu around 2560 BCE; it stayed the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years. Lehner 1997, The Complete Pyramids Merer's diary found 2013 The oldest known inscribed papyri, recording limestone transport for the Great Pyramid. Tallet & Lehner 2021, The Red Sea Scrolls NEW Lost Nile branch ~64 km long Satellite radar and cores reveal a buried Nile branch running beside 31 pyramids, likely used to move materials. chunks.heading: The First Global Economy Crashes
chunks.text: 12 ~3,700 to 3,100 years ago The First Global Economy Crashes Copper from Cyprus, tin from far inland, amber from the Baltic: then the whole network fell apart. Hot debate. ~3,700 to 3,100 years ago The First Global Economy Crashes Copper from Cyprus, tin from far inland, amber from the Baltic: then the whole network fell apart. Hot debate You are there It is about 1300 BCE off the rocky cape of Uluburun in southwestern Türkiye, and a merchant ship is in trouble. She is roughly 15 metres long, built of cedar, and she is carrying the Bronze Age in her hold: about ten tonnes of copper in 354 flat 'oxhide' ingots, roughly a tonne of tin to turn it into bronze, some 175 ingots of blue and turquoise glass, logs of African blackwood, hippo and elephant ivory, amber probably from the Baltic, jars of terebinth resin, and a gold scarab bearing the name of Egypt's Queen Nefertiti. The cargo comes from lands stretching from Egypt and Canaan to Cyprus, Mycenaean Greece and beyond. The ship goes down in about 45 metres of water. In 1982 a young sponge diver describes seeing 'metal biscuits with ears' on the sea floor, and archaeologists spend eleven summers bringing her story back up. The numbers Uluburun cargo ~10 t copper, ~1 t tin The right 10:1 ratio to make about 11 tonnes of bronze; the wreck dates to around 1300 BCE. chunks.heading: The Age of Big Questions
chunks.text: 13 800 to 200 BCE The Age of Big Questions Across Eurasia, people started asking what a good life is, and they also invented pocket change. Hot debate. 800 to 200 BCE The Age of Big Questions Across Eurasia, people started asking what a good life is, and they also invented pocket change. Hot debate You are there Sardis, capital of Lydia in western Anatolia, a little before 600 BCE. Grains of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, wash down the Pactolus stream, and Lydian craftsmen have learned to turn them into something new: small lumps of standard weight, struck with a punch and stamped with a lion's head. A trader no longer has to weigh metal at every deal. He can count. Within a few generations Lydian refiners are separating pure gold from pure silver, and the idea of the coin spreads through the Greek world, while China and India develop metal money of their own. In these same centuries, from Greek cities and Persian lands to the Ganges plain, the hills of Judah and the rival states of China, teachers and writers are asking restless questions about justice, suffering, duty and how to live. Did coins, cities and busy markets help make room for these new ideas? Historians are still arguing. The numbers 'Axial Age' 800–200 BCE Philosopher Karl Jaspers coined the term in 1949 for a burst of new thought across Eurasia. Jaspers 1949, Vom Ursprung und Ziel der Geschichte First coins ~630–600 BCE Stamped electrum pieces from Lydia and Ionia; Sardis later had a gold-refining workshop. chunks.heading: Empires and Long Roads
chunks.text: 14 ~550 BCE to 220 CE Empires and Long Roads Persia, Rome, the Mauryas and the Han built roads so good that ideas, silk and germs could travel them too. No receipts yet. ~550 BCE to 220 CE Empires and Long Roads Persia, Rome, the Mauryas and the Han built roads so good that ideas, silk and germs could travel them too. No receipts yet You are there In 126 BCE a battered traveller rides back into the Han capital, Chang'an. His name is Zhang Qian, and about thirteen years earlier he set out with roughly a hundred companions on a mission for Emperor Wu: find the Yuezhi people in the far west and recruit them against the Xiongnu. It went badly. The Xiongnu captured him and held him for about ten years; he married there and had a son. He escaped, reached the Yuezhi, failed to persuade them, was captured again, and escaped again. Of the original party, only he and one companion make it home. But Zhang Qian brings back something more valuable than an alliance: reports of Ferghana and its magnificent horses, of Bactria's markets where he saw cloth and bamboo from southwest China that had come by way of India, and of Parthia and lands beyond. The court listens. Within decades Han envoys and caravans are heading west, and the web of routes later nicknamed the Silk Road is humming. The numbers Achaemenid Persia ~5.5 million km² At its height around 500 BCE, one of the largest empires of the ancient world. chunks.heading: Faiths, Plagues and a Dim Sun
chunks.text: 15 ~300 to 950 CE Faiths, Plagues and a Dim Sun New faiths spread across continents while volcanoes, plague and drought tested every empire. Hot debate. ~300 to 950 CE Faiths, Plagues and a Dim Sun New faiths spread across continents while volcanoes, plague and drought tested every empire. Hot debate You are there Constantinople, 536 CE. The historian Procopius notices something eerie and writes it down: for the whole year, he says, the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon. Far to the west, Irish annals will record a 'failure of bread'. Ice cores show why: a large volcanic eruption that year filled the northern sky with sulphate haze, and another followed around 540. Tree rings across the Northern Hemisphere record some of the coldest summers of the last two thousand years. Then, in 541, a new terror arrives by ship at Pelusium in Egypt: plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It reaches Constantinople the next year. Procopius, still writing, claims that at the peak ten thousand people a day are dying in the city. Historians argue over that number and over how deadly the pandemic was across the whole Mediterranean. They agree it was a frightening time to be alive, and that the people living through it had no idea the two disasters were linked to faraway volcanoes and fleas. The numbers 536 CE eruption eruptions in 536 and ~540 Ice cores reveal two eruptions that caused one of the sharpest Northern Hemisphere coolings of the last two millennia. Sigl et al. 2015, Nature Late Antique Little Ice Age ~536–660 CE Tree rings show a cool period lasting over a century after the eruptions. chunks.heading: The World Joins Up
chunks.text: 16 ~900 to 1500 CE The World Joins Up Norse ships, Polynesian canoes, camel caravans and Chinese paper money: the planet was getting connected. No receipts yet. ~900 to 1500 CE The World Joins Up Norse ships, Polynesian canoes, camel caravans and Chinese paper money: the planet was getting connected. No receipts yet You are there The northern tip of Newfoundland, the year 1021. Norse voyagers from Greenland have built turf halls around timber frames near a shallow bay, and today someone is cutting wood with an iron blade, leaving clean, flat cuts that no stone tool would make. They have no idea the wood carries a hidden timestamp. In 993 a burst of cosmic radiation, most likely from a storm on the Sun, left a spike of radiocarbon in every tree growing that year. A thousand years later, scientists count the rings outward from that spike to the bark edge on three pieces of wood from three different trees, and each one was felled in 1021. The Norse do not stay long; the sagas describe voyages to a land called Vinland and tense meetings with the people already living there. But for a moment, as far as we know, human journeys have looped all the way around the planet: travellers who came west across the Atlantic meet the descendants of people who came east into the Americas from Asia. chunks.heading: Everyone Remembers the Flood. The Rocks Do Not.
chunks.text: Flood Everyone Remembers the Flood. The Rocks Do Not. Primeval age (setting); texts c. 1700 BCE onward Busted. Flood Everyone Remembers the Flood. The Rocks Do Not. Primeval age (setting); texts c. 1700 BCE onward. Told by: Mesopotamian, Hebrew Bible, Greek, Hindu. Busted A single flood covered the whole Earth within the span of human history. The story The account. Atrahasis; Epic of Gilgamesh Tablet XI; Genesis 6-9; Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1; Deucalion in Apollodorus. Written: Atrahasis c. 1700 BCE; Genesis flood strands probably 1st millennium BCE; Shatapatha Brahmana c. 800-500 BCE A divine decision to wipe the world clean, one favoured man warned in advance, a boat stocked with living things, and a landing on a mountain. The Babylonian Utnapishtim sends out birds; Noah does the same; the Hindu Manu is towed to safety by a fish that grows enormous; the Greek Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulate the Earth by throwing stones over their shoulders. The shared skeleton is striking, and the Mesopotamian versions are the oldest written ones. The flood then swept away all these creatures, and Manu alone remained here. Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1.6, trans. Julius Eggeling (1882) The evidence Greenland ice cores preserve unbroken annual layers counted back some 60,000 years; a planet-wide sea over the ice sheet would have left a break that is not there. chunks.heading: Atlantis: The Island That Sank Into a Footnote
chunks.text: Lost city Atlantis: The Island That Sank Into a Footnote c. 9600 BCE (setting); told c. 360 BCE Busted. Lost city Atlantis: The Island That Sank Into a Footnote c. 9600 BCE (setting); told c. 360 BCE. Told by: Greek. Busted A large island civilisation in the Atlantic sank around 9600 BCE. The story The account. Plato, Timaeus 24e-25d and Critias. Written: c. 360 BCE Plato has Critias relay a story said to come from Egyptian priests via the Athenian lawgiver Solon: 9,000 years earlier, a mighty island empire beyond the Pillars of Heracles attacked the Mediterranean world, was repelled by a heroic ancient Athens, and then vanished beneath the sea in a single day and night of earthquakes and floods. Plato uses the tale to illustrate his ideal state. No earlier writer mentions Atlantis. the island of Atlantis in like manner disappeared in the depths of the sea. Plato, Timaeus 25d, trans. chunks.heading: The Laetoli footprint makers
chunks.text: Laetoli, Tanzania The Laetoli footprint makers A few upright walkers crossed a field of wet volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago, and their stride is still there. 3.66M yrs ago. Laetoli, Tanzania The Laetoli footprint makers A few upright walkers crossed a field of wet volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago, and their stride is still there. 3.66M yrs ago The first walkers whose actual steps we can follow about 3.66 million years ago In 1976, at Laetoli in northern Tanzania, a playful fight with dried elephant dung sent the researcher Andrew Hill diving to the ground, where he noticed animal tracks pressed into hardened ash. The search that followed, led by Mary Leakey, uncovered in 1978 what she had hoped for: a trail of about 70 hominin footprints stretching some 24 metres at Site G. They were made about 3.66 million years ago, after ash from a nearby eruption was dampened by light rain and then set almost like cement. At least two walkers left the trail, and a third probably stepped into the prints of one of them. Heel strikes, raised arches and big toes in line with the other toes show upright striding. The story keeps growing. In 2015 a new trail at Site S revealed an individual nicknamed S1 who may have stood about 165 cm, much taller than Lucy, hinting at large size differences within the species. In 2019 a team re-excavated odd tracks at Site A, first uncovered in 1976 and once blamed on a bear. They concluded a hominin made them, walking with a cross-over step, which suggests more than one kind of biped shared this landscape. What we actually have Hominin trackways in the Footprint Tuff at Laetoli Sites G, S and A, plus casts, photographs and 3D scans. How we know Radiometric dating of the volcanic tuffs; footprint shape compared with humans, other primates and bear

chunks.text: Hadar, Ethiopia Lucy (AL 288-1), also called Dinkinesh She is the most famous skeleton on Earth, and much of what people think they know about her is wrong. 3.2M yrs ago. Hadar, Ethiopia Lucy (AL 288-1), also called Dinkinesh She is the most famous skeleton on Earth, and much of what people think they know about her is wrong. 3.2M yrs ago Celebrity fossil who never asked to be the 'missing link' about 3.2 million years ago On 24 November 1974, Donald Johanson and Tom Gray spotted a piece of arm bone in a gully at Hadar, Ethiopia. Over the following weeks the team recovered several hundred bone fragments from one individual, about 40 percent of a skeleton. That night the camp played the Beatles' 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' over and over, and the name stuck. In Ethiopia she is Dinkinesh, 'you are marvelous'. She stood about 1.1 metres tall, weighed perhaps 29 kg, and walked upright, while keeping long, strong arms useful for climbing. Now, what she was not. She was not the 'missing link': human evolution is a branching bush, not a chain. She was not the oldest hominin; older ones, such as Ardipithecus, are known. She was probably not alone: other hominin species likely shared the region at around the same time. And her death is an open case. A 2016 CT study argued that her unhealed fractures fit a fall from a tall tree; critics answer that many breaks could have formed long after death, as the bones fossilized and eroded. In 2025 she left Ethiopia for her first European exhibition, in Prague. What we actually have Several hundred fragments of a single skeleton (about 40 percent complete), held at the National Museum of Ethiopia, Addis Ababa. Nariokotome, Kenya The Nariokotome boy (KNM-WT 15000, 'Turkana Boy') The icon of early human long-distance walking was a child, probably with a toothache. 1.5M yrs ago Homo erectus kid with a sore back and a bad tooth about 1.5 million years ago In August 1984 Kamoya Kimeu, the celebrated fossil finder of the National Museums of Kenya, spotted a small piece of skull on a slope near the Nariokotome River, west of Lake Turkana. Excavations led by Richard Leakey and Alan Walker grew it into the most complete early human skeleton then known: about 1.5 million years old and assigned to Homo erectus (some call it Homo ergaster). He was young. His teeth were still coming in, and studies of tooth growth lines suggest he was probably around 8 years old, although estimates have ranged from about 7 to 12, because his species likely grew up faster than we do. He was already tall for his age, long-legged and narrow-hipped, a body plan suited to walking in heat. Early estimates had him becoming a 180 cm giant; later work suggests a more modest adult height. His lower jaw shows signs of infection, and a 2013 re-study argued that his spine reflects a herniated disc rather than a growth disorder, as had once been proposed. So one of the best-known fossils of our lineage is probably best imagined as a lanky, sore-backed kid with a bad tooth. chunks.text: Denisova Cave, Russia Denny (Denisova 11) A bone splinter the size of a thumbnail revealed a girl whose parents came from two different human groups. 90,000 yrs ago. Denisova Cave, Russia Denny (Denisova 11) A bone splinter the size of a thumbnail revealed a girl whose parents came from two different human groups. 90,000 yrs ago Daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father about 90,000 years ago Denisova Cave in Siberia has produced thousands of bone scraps too broken to identify by eye. Researchers screened them with ZooMS, a method that fingerprints the collagen protein in bone, and in 2016 reported that one splinter, among roughly 2,000 fragments, came from a hominin rather than a mammoth or a bear. It was only about 2.5 cm long. Its genome, published in 2018, told one of the most surprising family stories in science. This individual, a girl at least 13 years old, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father: not distant mixed ancestry, but first-generation parents from two different groups. Her father's own genome carried traces of an earlier Neanderthal ancestor, so meetings like this had happened before. Her mother was genetically closer to Neanderthals who lived later in Croatia than to an earlier Neanderthal from the same Siberian cave, which hints that Neanderthal populations moved across Eurasia. Denny lived roughly 90,000 years ago. We have no face, no grave and no tools linked to her; just a sliver of long bone that changed estimates of how often these groups met and had children. Shanidar Cave, Iraq Shanidar Z Her skull had been flattened to about 2 cm thick; scientists put her face back together piece by piece. 75,000 yrs ago Neanderthal woman rebuilt from 200 fragments about 75,000 years ago In 2018, working at Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan for the first time in about half a century, a team led by Cambridge researchers found the upper body of a Neanderthal. Her skull had been crushed in the ground to roughly 2 cm thick. Conservator Lucia Lopez-Polin strengthened the fragile pieces on site, and in the lab more than 200 fragments were reassembled, a high-stakes 3D jigsaw. Proteins in her tooth enamel point to a female; heavy wear, with front teeth ground down to the roots, suggests she died in her mid-40s, about 75,000 years ago. She stood roughly 150 cm tall and had some of the smallest adult arm bones in the Neanderthal record. She lay on her side with her left hand under her head, with a rock behind the head, within a cluster of burials beside a tall vertical rock. She lies close to Shanidar 4, the famous 'flower burial' reported in the 1960s. A 2023 study argues that the pollen there was most likely carried in by burrowing bees rather than left by mourners. The flowers may be gone, but the pattern of repeated burial at one spot still suggests these Neanderthals returned to, and remembered, their dead. What we actually have A crushed skull and upper skeleton excavated in 2018, reconstructed from more than 200 fragments. How we know Enamel peptide analysis for sex; dental wear for age; stratigraphy and luminescence dating of the cave deposits; palynology and bee-burrow analysis for the pollen

Lake Mungo, Australia Mungo Lady (Lake Mungo 1) Forty thousand years ago, on the shore of a lake that no longer exists, people cremated a young woman with care. 40,000 yrs ago Woman at the centre of one of the oldest known cremations about 40,000 years ago In July 1968 the geologist Jim Bowler was mapping ancient shorelines in the dry Willandra Lakes of New South Wales when he noticed burnt bone weathering out of a sand dune at Lake Mungo. The remains were of a young woman. Her body had been burned, the bones broken, and then burned again before being placed in a small pit: one of the oldest known cremations anywhere. In 1974, nearby, Bowler found a man buried on his back with his hands clasped, his body sprinkled with red ochre. Dating arguments ran for decades, with estimates from under 30,000 to over 60,000 years. A 2003 multi-method study placed both burials at about 40,000 years old, which makes these among the oldest funeral rituals known for modern humans. Her story also belongs to the present. Mungo Lady was returned to her Traditional Owners, the Paakantyi, Mutthi Mutthi and Ngiyampaa peoples, in 1992; Mungo Man was returned in 2015 and brought home to Lake Mungo in 2017. For these communities she is an ancestor, not a specimen, and her return reshaped how Australian science works with Aboriginal people and their dead. What we actually have Burnt and fragmented skeletal remains from a small pit in the Mungo lunette, plus the nearby ochre burial of Mungo Man. Rouffignac, France The children of the Ice Age caves Some of the marks in France's painted caves were made by toddlers, probably held up by an adult to reach the ceiling. 17,000–13,000 yrs ago Toddlers who drew on ceilings and teenagers who fetched clay about 17,000 to 13,000 years ago In Rouffignac Cave in the Dordogne, probably around 13,000 years ago, people dragged soft fingers through the clay of a chamber ceiling, leaving looping lines called flutings. Kevin Sharpe and Leslie Van Gelder measured the width of three-finger marks and compared them with flutings made by modern volunteers. They concluded that some ceiling marks were made by children about 2 to 5 years old. Given the height of the ceiling, the smallest artists were probably lifted by adults. In 2013 three expert San trackers from Namibia, invited by the Tracking in Caves project, read Ice Age prints in caves of the French Pyrenees. At Tuc d'Audoubert they identified a man of about 38 and a boy of about 14 walking on their heels near a clay pit, probably gathering clay for the famous modelled bison about 15 metres away. At Niaux they read one set of prints as those of a girl of about 12, although those prints are not securely dated. Children were not just tagging along; they were probably taking part. chunks.text: Hoyo Negro, Mexico Naia (Hoyo Negro 5/48) A teenage girl fell into a pitch-black pit at the end of the Ice Age; divers found her lying among saber-toothed cats. 13,000–12,000 yrs ago. Hoyo Negro, Mexico Naia (Hoyo Negro 5/48) A teenage girl fell into a pitch-black pit at the end of the Ice Age; divers found her lying among saber-toothed cats. 13,000–12,000 yrs ago Teenager who helped link the first Americans to living Native peoples about 13,000 to 12,000 years ago Around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, on the Yucatan Peninsula, a teenage girl walked through a dry cave system in the dark, probably searching for water. She fell into a deep pit now called Hoyo Negro, 'black hole'. Later, as the Ice Age ended and sea levels rose, the caves flooded. In 2007 cave divers exploring the drowned passages found her skeleton on the pit floor alongside the bones of saber-toothed cats, giant ground sloths and other animals that had made the same fatal mistake. Researchers named her Naia, after water nymphs. She was about 15 or 16. Her mitochondrial DNA belongs to a lineage (D1) found among living Native Americans, while her skull has the long, narrow shape typical of early Paleoamericans. Together these support the idea that the first Americans and today's Indigenous peoples share ancestry despite differences in appearance. Later analyses, presented at a 2017 conference, suggest she was small and slender, went through repeated periods of hunger, and may have given birth before she died. Hers was likely a hard and mobile life, cut short by a single misstep in the dark. What we actually have A nearly complete skeleton recovered from an underwater pit, with associated Ice Age animal bones. How we know Radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dating of tooth enamel and cave mineral deposits; mitocho

chunks.heading: Otzi the Iceman
chunks.text: Tisenjoch, Italy Otzi the Iceman Hikers thought they had found a recent climber; he had been lying in the ice for 5,300 years, with an arrowhead in his shoulder. 5,300 yrs ago. Tisenjoch, Italy Otzi the Iceman Hikers thought they had found a recent climber; he had been lying in the ice for 5,300 years, with an arrowhead in his shoulder. 5,300 yrs ago Copper Age traveller, murder victim and the most studied body on Earth about 5,300 years ago (c. 3350 to 3100 BCE) On 19 September 1991, hikers Erika and Helmut Simon saw a brown body emerging from melting ice high in the Otztal Alps and assumed he was an unlucky modern climber. He had died about 5,300 years ago. Surveyors later placed the spot 92.56 metres inside Italy, which is why he now rests in a museum in Bolzano. For a decade he seemed to have died of exposure; then, in 2001, X-rays revealed a stone arrowhead in his left shoulder. He also had a head injury. His stomach, analysed in 2018, held a last meal eaten between half an hour and two hours before death: very fatty ibex meat, red deer, einkorn wheat and traces of bracken. The copper of his axe came from southern Tuscany. His 61 tattoos, a 2024 experimental study argues, were most likely hand-poked rather than cut. And a 2023 genome re-analysis changed his look: he probably had dark skin, dark eyes and male-pattern baldness, and more than 90 percent of his ancestry came from early farmers with roots in Anatolia. The pale, shaggy Iceman of older museum reconstructions reflected modern assumptions more than his DNA. What we actually have A naturally mummified body with clothing, a copper axe, a bow, arrows, a dagger and other gear. How we know Radiocarbon dating; X-ray and CT imaging; stomach-content analysis (proteomics, lipids, DNA, microscopy); lead-isotope sourc

chunks.heading: Kushim
chunks.text: Uruk, southern Iraq Kushim The first individual whose name we may be able to read left no poem, no battle and no face; just a receipt. 3200–3000 BCE. Uruk, southern Iraq Kushim The first individual whose name we may be able to read left no poem, no battle and no face; just a receipt. 3200–3000 BCE Possibly the first named person in history, and possibly an accountant about 3200 to 3000 BCE Around 3200 to 3000 BCE, in the city of Uruk in what is now southern Iraq, administrators pressed signs into small clay tablets. The earliest writing, called proto-cuneiform, was not yet used for letters or poems; it was bookkeeping. One tablet, now in the Schoyen Collection, records a large total of barley over 37 months and ends with two signs read KU and SHIM. The same combination appears on about 18 tablets. Yuval Noah Harari's bestseller Sapiens made the reading famous, rendering it as 29,086 measures of barley, signed Kushim. Specialists are more cautious. The signs could be a personal name, but they could also be a job title or the name of an office, because the earliest script rarely made the difference clear. The texts linked to Kushim deal with barley and grain products, probably connected with the malting and brewing work of a large institution. If Kushim was a person, then the first name we can read belongs not to a king but to someone checking that the numbers added up. That is a rather reassuring start for written history. What we actually have Proto-cuneiform clay tablets from Uruk (for example MS 1717 in the Schoyen Collection) bearing the sign sequence KU.SHIM. How we know Decipherment of proto-cuneiform numerical systems and administrative formats, comparing sign use across hundreds of archaic tablets. A rival for the 'oldest known name', Gal-Sal, appears on a tablet

chunks.heading: Merer, inspector of boatmen
chunks.text: Tura quarries and Giza, Egypt Merer, inspector of boatmen The oldest inscribed papyri ever found are not royal decrees; they are the work diary of a mid-level boss hauling stone for the Great Pyramid. 2560 BCE. Tura quarries and Giza, Egypt Merer, inspector of boatmen The oldest inscribed papyri ever found are not royal decrees; they are the work diary of a mid-level boss hauling stone for the Great Pyramid. 2560 BCE Middle manager whose logbook tracks work on the Great Pyramid about 2560 BCE (reign of Khufu, year 27) In 2013, at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbour on Egypt's Red Sea coast, a team led by Pierre Tallet and Gregory Marouard found papyrus rolls left at the entrance of storage galleries cut into the rock. They are the oldest inscribed papyri known, from late in the reign of King Khufu, around 2560 BCE. Among them is the logbook of an inspector named Merer, who led a crew of about 40 boatmen. His entries are laid out day by day in neat columns, recording a steady rhythm: loading limestone at the Tura quarries across the Nile, sailing to Akhet-Khufu, 'Horizon of Khufu', the ancient name for the Great Pyramid site at Giza, stopping overnight at places such as the She-Khufu basin, and heading back for more. The fine Tura limestone was probably destined for the pyramid's outer casing. Merer also mentions Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother, as the official in charge of a harbour at Giza. No pharaoh speaks in these pages, and there are no secret machines; just a supervisor counting trips and days. It is the closest thing we have to a worker's view of the Great Pyramid in its final years of construction. What we actually have Fragments of papyrus logbooks (the 'Diary of Merer') found at Wadi al-Jarf, now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo. How we know Hieratic palaeography and

chunks.heading: Puabi of Ur
chunks.text: Royal Cemetery, southern Iraq Puabi of Ur Her headdress of gold leaves is one of the most dazzling objects of the ancient world; the people buried around her tell a darker story. 2600–2500 BCE. Royal Cemetery, southern Iraq Puabi of Ur Her headdress of gold leaves is one of the most dazzling objects of the ancient world; the people buried around her tell a darker story. 2600–2500 BCE Queen or high lady buried in gold, and not alone about 2600 to 2500 BCE In the late 1920s, Leonard Woolley's excavators at Ur opened a tomb numbered PG 800 and found a woman on a wooden bier, her upper body covered in beads of gold, silver, lapis lazuli and carnelian, with a spectacular headdress of gold leaves, ribbons and flowers. A lapis cylinder seal nearby named her Puabi, with the title nin, meaning 'queen' or 'lady'. Unusually, the seal names no husband, which likely signals that her rank stood on its own. She died around 2600 to 2500 BCE, probably at about 40 years old. She was not buried alone. Woolley recorded dozens of attendants in her burial complex, about 52 by one count, and imagined them calmly drinking poison. In 2011, CT scans of two skulls from other graves in the Royal Cemetery suggested a harsher end: blunt-force wounds, probably from a pointed, weighted weapon, plus signs of heating and traces of mercury sulphide, possibly used to slow decay while the bodies were laid out. Behind the glitter of the headdress sits a sobering question: what did royal display cost the people around it? What we actually have Tomb PG 800 with Puabi's skeleton, jewellery, headdress and inscribed cylinder seals, now largely at the Penn Museum, Philadelphia. How we know Excavation records; reading of the cuneiform seal inscription; later CT scanning and forensic analysis of skulls from the Roy

chunks.heading: Enheduanna
chunks.text: Ur, southern Iraq Enheduanna The first author known by name in world literature may have been a princess-priestess writing about her own exile. 2300–2250 BCE. Ur, southern Iraq Enheduanna The first author known by name in world literature may have been a princess-priestess writing about her own exile. 2300–2250 BCE Princess, high priestess and the first named author about 2300 to 2250 BCE Around 2300 BCE, Sargon of Akkad built the first great empire of Mesopotamia and installed his daughter as en-priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. She took, or was given, the name Enheduanna. In the 1920s Leonard Woolley's team at Ur found a calcite disk showing her at a ritual in a flounced robe, with an inscription naming her as Sargon's daughter. Her fame rests on poetry. Several Sumerian hymns, copied by scribes centuries later, name her as their author, which would make her the first named author in world literature. In the poem known as 'The Exaltation of Inana' she speaks in the first person: pushed out of her office during a revolt, she describes her exile with raw emotion and pleads with the goddess Inana to restore her. It is vivid, personal and startlingly angry. Scholars debate how much she composed herself, because the surviving copies are around 500 years younger than she is, and the attribution may partly reflect later tradition. Either way, Mesopotamian scribes chose to remember a woman as the voice behind some of their greatest hymns. I, En-hedu-ana the en priestess, entered my holy jipar in your service. The Exaltation of Inana (Inana B), ETCSL translation, University of Oxford What we actually have An inscribed calcite (alabaster) disk from Ur (Penn Museum) naming her; Old Babylonian clay-tablet copies of hymns attributed to her; seals of her servants. How we know

chunks.heading: Hammurabi of Babylon
chunks.text: Babylon, central Iraq Hammurabi of Babylon His famous law code was carried off as war loot, lost for three thousand years, and dug up in a different country. 1792–1750 BCE. Babylon, central Iraq Hammurabi of Babylon His famous law code was carried off as war loot, lost for three thousand years, and dug up in a different country. 1792–1750 BCE King who carved his idea of justice into stone reigned about 1792 to 1750 BCE Hammurabi ruled Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE and turned a mid-sized city-state into the leading power of Mesopotamia. Late in his reign he set up a tall black stone stele, over 2 metres high, topped by a carving of the king standing before a god usually identified as Shamash, the sun god and guardian of justice. Below it: a prologue, about 282 laws, and an epilogue inviting anyone wronged to come and have the inscription read to them. The laws are not an even-handed modern code. Penalties depend on social status: destroying the eye of a free man could cost an eye, while injuring a commoner or an enslaved person meant a payment. A builder whose badly built house collapsed and killed the owner could be put to death. Many scholars now read the collection less as a rulebook judges followed and more as a royal showcase of wise judgments. The stele had its own adventures: an Elamite king carried it to Susa as war booty in the 12th century BCE, and French excavators found it there in 1901 and 1902. Today it stands in the Louvre, still making its case to visitors. to bring about the rule of righteousness in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil-doers; so that the strong should not harm the weak Prologue to the Laws of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King (1910) What we actually have The basalt stele in the Louvre, fragments of other copies, and later clay-t

chunks.heading: Ea-nasir and Nanni
chunks.text: Ur, southern Iraq Ea-nasir and Nanni The oldest known customer complaint was found in the house of the merchant it was aimed at. 1750 BCE. Ur, southern Iraq Ea-nasir and Nanni The oldest known customer complaint was found in the house of the merchant it was aimed at. 1750 BCE Copper merchant with a bad reputation, and his furious customer about 1750 BCE Around 1750 BCE, a man named Nanni in the city of Ur was fed up. He had dealt with Ea-nasir, a merchant who brought copper up the Gulf through Dilmun (modern Bahrain), and received ingots he considered below the agreed quality. Worse, he said his servant had been treated rudely and his money had not come back. So he had a clay tablet written, and it survives: a small letter about 11.6 cm tall, now in the British Museum. He complains that messengers he sent to collect his money came back empty-handed, several times, even through dangerous territory, and he demands to be treated with respect. The best twist: the tablet was found in Ea-nasir's own house at Ur during Leonard Woolley's excavations, alongside other letters grumbling about copper deliveries. Either Ea-nasir kept his complaints on file, or complaints were simply a large share of his business correspondence. Nearly 4,000 years later he has become an internet legend, a sort of patron saint of bad suppliers. The tablet is also a serious window onto long-distance metal trade, credit and business etiquette in the Old Babylonian world. What do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt? Nanni to Ea-nasir, UET V 81, trans. A. Leo Oppenheim, Letters from Mesopotamia (1967) What we actually have Clay tablet BM 131236 (UET V 81), written in Akkadian cuneiform, plus other letters from the same house at Ur. How we know Excavation context at Ur; deci

chunks.heading: Hatshepsut
chunks.text: Thebes, Egypt Hatshepsut She ruled Egypt as king for about twenty years; the smashing of her statues afterwards may not have been the revenge story we were told. 1479–1458 BCE. Thebes, Egypt Hatshepsut She ruled Egypt as king for about twenty years; the smashing of her statues afterwards may not have been the revenge story we were told. 1479–1458 BCE Queen who made herself king reigned about 1479 to 1458 BCE Hatshepsut was the daughter of one pharaoh, the wife of another, and regent for a third, the young Thutmose III. Then she did something unusual: she had herself crowned king. For about two decades she ruled with full royal titles and was often shown with a king's kilt and false beard. Her projects include the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri, whose reliefs celebrate an expedition to the distant land of Punt that returned with incense trees and exotic animals. After her death her images were broken and her name cut from monuments, long read as Thutmose III's revenge. A 2025 study of 1920s excavation archives suggests a cooler motive. Many statues were broken at weak points such as the neck, waist and knees in ways consistent with ritual 'deactivation', some faces were left intact, and the pieces were reused as building material. The erasure also came years into Thutmose's sole reign, which fits succession politics better than personal hatred. Even her body is debated: a mummy from tomb KV60 was identified as hers in 2007 on the basis of a tooth, but that match has not been confirmed by DNA and some scholars remain unconvinced. What we actually have Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri, obelisks at Karnak, hundreds of statue fragments, inscriptions, and a debated mummy (KV60-A). How we know Hieroglyphic inscriptions; archaeology of statue deposits and archival excavat

chunks.heading: Tutankhamun
chunks.text: Valley of the Kings, Egypt Tutankhamun Behind the golden mask was a young man who probably walked with a cane. 1323 BCE. Valley of the Kings, Egypt Tutankhamun Behind the golden mask was a young man who probably walked with a cane. 1323 BCE Teenage king whose body tells a story of illness died about 1323 BCE Howard Carter's 1922 discovery of a nearly intact royal tomb made Tutankhamun the world's most famous pharaoh, although he was a minor king who died young, around 1323 BCE. What does his body tell us? A 2010 study combining CT scans and DNA from royal mummies concluded that he died at about 19 and that his parents were probably brother and sister: the mummy from tomb KV55, most likely Akhenaten, and an unnamed woman known as the 'Younger Lady' from tomb KV35. The study reported a clubfoot, bone death in part of his left foot (Kohler disease II), a cleft palate, and DNA from the most dangerous malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. It proposed malaria combined with the bone disease as the most likely cause of death. His tomb held about 130 walking sticks and staves, some with signs of use, which fits a king who probably walked with pain. Treat the details with care: other researchers have questioned the ancient DNA methods and some diagnoses, and a broken leg remains debated as either injury or damage from embalming or excavation. The golden mask covered a young man who was probably often unwell. What we actually have His mummy, CT data, DNA samples, and the contents of tomb KV62, including about 130 sticks and staves. How we know CT scanning, ancient DNA (Y-chromosome and autosomal markers) for kinship, pathogen DNA testing, and study of the tomb objects. Two mummified foetuses buried in his tomb may have been his daughters, according to the same 2010 DNA study.

chunks.heading: The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht)
chunks.text: Deir el-Medina, Egypt The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht) When the grain rations were late, the pharaoh's tomb builders put down their tools and walked out. 1157 BCE. Deir el-Medina, Egypt The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht) When the grain rations were late, the pharaoh's tomb builders put down their tools and walked out. 1157 BCE Royal tomb workers who staged the first recorded strike about 1157 BCE (year 29 of Ramesses III) The craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings lived in their own walled village, Deir el-Medina, and were paid in rations of grain. In year 29 of Ramesses III, around 1157 BCE, those rations were badly overdue. So the crew did something no earlier record shows: they stopped work and walked out. The scribe Amennakht kept notes, which survive on a papyrus now in Turin. The workers marched past the guard posts of the necropolis, sat down behind temples on the west bank, and refused to go back, insisting their grievance be reported to Pharaoh. Officials delivered rations; the crew returned; supplies slipped again; they struck again. The dispute stretched over several months. For the officials it was an embarrassment. For historians it is priceless: a record of ordinary workers in a powerful state organizing, negotiating and getting at least part of what they were owed. The village was unusually literate, and its rubbish heaps have yielded thousands of inscribed potsherds and limestone flakes, including a register of work absences whose excuses range from illness to brewing beer. On this day the crew passed the five guard-posts of the tomb saying: 'We are hungry.' Turin Strike Papyrus, trans. P. J. Frandsen, 'Editing Reality: The Turin Strike Papyrus' (1990) What we actuall

chunks.heading: Tollund Man
chunks.text: Bjaeldskovdal bog, Denmark Tollund Man His face looked so fresh that the peat cutters who found him called the police. 405–380 BCE. Bjaeldskovdal bog, Denmark Tollund Man His face looked so fresh that the peat cutters who found him called the police. 405–380 BCE Iron Age man with a peaceful face and a noose around his neck about 405 to 380 BCE On 8 May 1950, peat cutters near Silkeborg in Denmark uncovered a face so well preserved that they called the police, fearing a recent death. He had died around 405 to 380 BCE. The acidic, oxygen-poor bog had tanned his skin and preserved his head in extraordinary detail: closed eyes, short-cropped hair and a faint stubble. He wore a pointed skin cap and a belt, and around his neck was a plaited leather noose. He was about 40 and had been hanged, then laid in an old peat cutting in a curled, sleeping position. Many archaeologists interpret him as a sacrifice, although the reasons remain uncertain. A 2021 re-examination of his gut found that his last meal, eaten roughly 12 to 24 hours before death, was a porridge made mainly of barley, pale persicaria seeds and flax, with some fish. He also carried whipworm, roundworm and tapeworm. The researchers found nothing obviously festive or special about the meal. A ritual death, then, but perhaps preceded by an ordinary day's food, which makes him feel even closer to us. What we actually have A bog body whose head is exceptionally well preserved, with the noose, cap and belt; gut contents. How we know Radiocarbon dating; autopsy, X-ray and CT scanning; macrofossil, pollen, protein and parasite analysis of gut contents. At Silkeborg Museum his head is original, but most of the body on display is a replica, because only parts of it were conserved in 1950.

chunks.heading: Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai)
chunks.text: Mawangdui, China Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai) Her body was so well preserved that doctors could perform an autopsy 2,100 years after she died, and they found melon seeds in her stomach. 168 BCE. Mawangdui, China Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai) Her body was so well preserved that doctors could perform an autopsy 2,100 years after she died, and they found melon seeds in her stomach. 168 BCE Han dynasty noblewoman with a modern-looking medical file died about 168 BCE In 1972, at Mawangdui near Changsha, archaeologists excavated Tomb 1, a deep Han dynasty grave sealed with thick layers of charcoal and white clay. Inside four nested coffins, in a mysterious liquid, lay Xin Zhui, wife of Li Cang, Marquis of Dai and chancellor of the Changsha kingdom. She had died around 168 BCE, at about 50, and her body was astonishingly preserved: soft skin, joints that could still bend, hair still in place. The autopsy reads like a modern medical file. She had hardened coronary arteries, gallstones, spinal problems that probably caused back pain, and schistosomiasis, a parasitic infection. In her digestive tract were more than a hundred melon seeds, suggesting she ate melon a few hours before a heart attack killed her, probably in summer. She was buried with over a thousand objects, including silk garments, lacquerware, food and a painted T-shaped silk banner that depicts a journey from the underworld to the heavens. Her body suggests the privileged life of a Han noblewoman also brought diseases we still link to rich diets and little exercise. What we actually have A remarkably preserved body, her tomb furnishings and a painted silk banner, now in the Hunan Museum, Changsha. How we know Modern medical autopsy and pathology (1972); study of tomb inscriptions and seals naming he

chunks.heading: The graffiti writers of Pompeii
chunks.text: Pompeii, Italy The graffiti writers of Pompeii Pompeii's walls were its social media, and one ancient writer complained that there was too much of it. up–79 CE. Pompeii, Italy The graffiti writers of Pompeii Pompeii's walls were its social media, and one ancient writer complained that there was too much of it. up–79 CE A whole town of scribblers, gossips and election campaigners up to 79 CE When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE it froze a town whose walls were covered in writing. Archaeologists have recorded thousands of painted notices and scratched graffiti: election endorsements, gladiator fan messages, greetings to friends, love notes, insults, sums and occasional crude boasts. One line, found in the Basilica, the Theatre and the Amphitheatre, is a joke about the whole scene: the wall deserves praise for not collapsing under so much boring writing. Graffiti were not mainly vandalism; studies of houses show messages answering one another, like comment threads. And the walls still make news. In 2018 a charcoal note in a house under renovation at the time of the eruption recorded a date equal to 17 October. The year is not written, but it supports other evidence, such as autumn fruits and lit braziers, that the eruption came later than the traditional 24 August. In January 2026, a Sorbonne-led team using reflectance transformation imaging, which lights a surface from many angles, announced 79 previously unknown graffiti in the corridor leading to the theatres, including a declaration of love and a drawing of two gladiators. Admiror, paries, te non cecidisse ruinis, qui tot scriptorum taedia sustineas. (I wonder, wall, that you have not fallen in ruins, bearing the tedious scribbles of so many writers.) chunks.heading: Claudia Severa
chunks.text: Vindolanda, UK Claudia Severa The earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman is the end of a birthday invitation. 97–105 CE. Vindolanda, UK Claudia Severa The earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman is the end of a birthday invitation. 97–105 CE Officer's wife who sent a birthday invitation on the Roman frontier about 97 to 105 CE Around 100 CE, at the Roman fort of Vindolanda in northern Britain (Hadrian's Wall came a couple of decades later), Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the commander Flavius Cerialis, received a thin wooden leaf tablet written in ink. It came from her friend Claudia Severa, wife of Aelius Brocchus, who commanded a fort nearby. The message: please come to my birthday celebration on 11 September; it will make the day more enjoyable. Most of the letter was written by a scribe. At the end, a different hand adds a personal farewell. Scholars identify this as Claudia herself, which makes these lines among the earliest known examples of Latin written by a woman. The tablet was excavated in 1985, one of hundreds of documents preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-free layers at Vindolanda, alongside requests for beer, lists that mention socks, and a report sneering at the 'Brittunculi', the 'wretched little Britons'. What survives here is not grand history but friendship on a cold frontier: two women arranging a party, and one of them adding her own words. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul, as I hope to prosper, and hail. Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, Tab. Vindol. 291, trans. A. K. Bowman and J. D. Thomas What we actually have Vindolanda tablet 291, a wooden leaf tablet written in ink, now in the British Museum (1986,1001.64). chunks.heading: Hypatia of Alexandria
chunks.text: Alexandria, Egypt Hypatia of Alexandria She was the most respected teacher in a great city of learning, until local politics turned lethal. March 415 CE. Alexandria, Egypt Hypatia of Alexandria She was the most respected teacher in a great city of learning, until local politics turned lethal. March 415 CE Mathematician, astronomer and philosopher died March 415 CE Hypatia taught in Alexandria in the late 300s and early 400s CE, a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher in a city famous for learning. Her father Theon was a mathematician who edited Euclid and wrote on Ptolemy; a heading in his commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest credits Hypatia with revising the text of one book. Later sources say she wrote commentaries on Diophantus's Arithmetica and Apollonius's Conics, though none survive clearly under her name. What survives best is her reputation. Her student Synesius, later a bishop, wrote her admiring letters, including one asking her to have a hydroscope, an instrument for weighing liquids, made for him. The church historian Socrates Scholasticus, writing a generation later, praised her learning and her public standing among the city's officials. In March 415, amid a bitter feud between the city's prefect Orestes and its bishop Cyril, a mob seized her in the street, dragged her into a church and killed her. Modern films and slogans have turned her into many symbols. The ancient sources show something more human: a brilliant teacher caught in local power struggles. made such attainments in literature and science, as to far surpass all the philosophers of her own time. Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History 7.15, trans. A. C. Zenos (1890) What we actually have No body and none of her own writings securely survive; the evidence is textual: Synesius's letters to

chunks.heading: K'inich Janaab Pakal of Palenque
chunks.text: Palenque, Mexico K'inich Janaab Pakal of Palenque The inscriptions said he died at 80; his skeleton seemed to say 40; the argument took half a century to settle. 603–683 CE. Palenque, Mexico K'inich Janaab Pakal of Palenque The inscriptions said he died at 80; his skeleton seemed to say 40; the argument took half a century to settle. 603–683 CE Maya king who ruled for 68 years 603 to 683 CE K'inich Janaab Pakal was born in 603 CE and crowned king of the Maya city of Palenque in 615, at the age of 12, after a turbulent period in which his mother, Sak K'uk', held power. He ruled for 68 years, long enough to rebuild a battered kingdom into one of the most elegant cities of the Classic Maya world. His funerary monument, the Temple of the Inscriptions, carries one of the longest Maya hieroglyphic texts. In 1948 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed a floor slab with holes for lifting it and found a rubble-filled staircase leading down into the pyramid. Clearing it took years. In 1952 he reached a crypt with a huge carved sarcophagus lid and a skeleton wearing a jade mosaic mask. Then came a puzzle: the inscriptions said Pakal died at 80, but the teeth suggested someone of 40 to 50. Decades of debate followed. A bioarchaeological team led by Vera Tiesler, working from 1999 to 2003, concluded the bones fit an elderly man; his soft, refined royal diet had probably spared his teeth. The texts, it seems, were right. What we actually have His skeleton, sarcophagus, jade mask and tomb in the Temple of the Inscriptions, plus hieroglyphic texts recording his life dates. How we know Decipherment of Maya hieroglyphs and calendar dates; skeletal ageing methods; bioarchaeological analysis of the tomb. His jade death mask was stolen from Mexico's National Museum of Anthropology

chunks.heading: The Birka warrior of grave Bj 581
chunks.text: Birka, Sweden The Birka warrior of grave Bj 581 For a century she was the textbook Viking warrior, assumed to be a man; then her DNA was read. mid-900s CE. Birka, Sweden The Birka warrior of grave Bj 581 For a century she was the textbook Viking warrior, assumed to be a man; then her DNA was read. mid-900s CE Viking-age woman buried with a full warrior's kit mid-900s CE In the 1870s Hjalmar Stolpe excavated a chamber grave at Birka, a Viking-age trading town on an island in Lake Malaren, Sweden. Grave Bj 581, from the mid-900s, held one person buried with a sword, an axe, two spears, armour-piercing arrows, two shields, two horses and a gaming set with pieces and dice. For more than a century it served as the model of a high-status Viking warrior, assumed to be male. In 2016 the osteologist Anna Kjellstrom re-examined the skeleton and found female traits; in 2017 a genomic study found two X chromosomes and no Y. Isotopes suggest she was not born at Birka, and she was over 30 when she died. The reaction was huge, and so was the criticism. Had the bones been mixed up since the 19th century? Were the weapons gifts for someone who never fought? In 2019 the team replied, rechecking the excavation records and arguing the skeleton belongs to the grave. They left open whether she was a fighting warrior, a symbolic one or something else. The debate now centres less on her sex and more on how archaeologists read gender into grave goods for a century. What we actually have Chamber grave Bj 581 with its skeleton, weapons, horses and gaming set, documented in Stolpe's records and stored in Stockholm. How we know Osteology; ancient DNA (sex chromosomes and mitochondrial DNA); strontium isotopes for mobility; re-examination of 19th-century excavation plans. The gaming set placed on he

chunks.heading: Mansa Musa of Mali
chunks.text: Mali Empire, West Africa Mansa Musa of Mali He arrived in Cairo with so much gold that, according to one chronicler, the price of gold fell. 1312–1337 CE. Mali Empire, West Africa Mansa Musa of Mali He arrived in Cairo with so much gold that, according to one chronicler, the price of gold fell. 1312–1337 CE Emperor whose gold made headlines in Cairo and Europe ruled about 1312 to 1337 CE; journey to Cairo in 1324 In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa, crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca and stopped in Cairo. He came with a huge caravan and, by every account, astonishing quantities of gold. The Damascus-born official al-Umari, writing about a dozen years later using interviews with Cairo officials who had met him, reports that Musa showered gold on courtiers and office holders, and that his people spent so freely that the value of gold in Egypt fell. He also reports a court drama: told to kiss the ground before the Mamluk sultan, Musa at first refused. The visit made Mali famous far beyond Africa; the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows a West African king holding a gold nugget. Modern claims that Musa was the richest person who ever lived are guesses, since no figure can be calculated. And the historian Warren Schultz, checking Cairo exchange-rate records, found the gold slump real but temporary, not the twelve-year crash al-Umari describes. Even so, the episode shows West African gold at the heart of the medieval world economy. They exchanged gold until they depressed its value in Egypt and caused its price to fall. al-Umari, Masalik al-absar, trans. in N. Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981) What we actually have Arabic chronicles (al-Umari, Ibn Khaldun, al-Maqrizi and others), Cairo exchange

chunks.heading: Pyramid Texts
chunks.text: Old Kingdom Egypt Pyramid Texts c. 2400-2300 BCE (carved); some spells likely older oral liturgy Rock solid. Old Kingdom Egypt Pyramid Texts c. 2400-2300 BCE (carved); some spells likely older oral liturgy Rock solid Language and script Old Egyptian; hieroglyphs carved and painted on stone walls Oldest copy Walls of the burial chamber and antechamber of the Pyramid of Unas, c. 2350 BCE (Unas's reign is dated anywhere from c. 2404-2374 to c. 2312-2282 BCE) Where it is now In situ, Saqqara, Egypt Size 283 spells in Unas's pyramid alone; hundreds more across later Old Kingdom pyramids Dating confidence high for the carvings, low for oral origins What it says A launch manual for a dead king. The spells help the pharaoh climb a ladder to the sky, ride a reed float across the heavens, join the boat of the sun god Ra and become one of the stars that never set. Others are practical charms against snakes and scorpions. The notorious Cannibal Hymn has the king swallowing gods to absorb their power. It reads less like a book than a ritual toolkit, carved in stone so it would keep working forever. History check The texts sit exactly where and when they appear to belong: inside securely identified royal pyramids at Saqqara (Unas, Teti, Pepi I, Merenre, Pepi II and several queens). Their content is religious, not a chronicle, but it matches temple and tomb evidence for Old Kingdom cults of Ra and Osiris. Absolute dates for Unas still vary by several decades between chronologies. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid As a record of Old Kingdom royal belief and ritual. Unas's burial chamber has a ceiling painted with golden stars. Until the 1880s, most scholars assumed pyramid interiors were blank; the carved spells were only discovered in 1880-81.

chunks.heading: Epic of Gilgamesh
chunks.text: Mesopotamia (Sumer and Babylonia) Epic of Gilgamesh Sumerian poems c. 2100 BCE; Old Babylonian epic c. 1800 BCE; Standard version (attributed to Sin-leqi-unninni) c. 1200-1100 BCE Mixed record. Mesopotamia (Sumer and Babylonia) Epic of Gilgamesh Sumerian poems c. 2100 BCE; Old Babylonian epic c. 1800 BCE; Standard version (attributed to Sin-leqi-unninni) c. 1200-1100 BCE Mixed record Language and script Sumerian (early poems) and Akkadian (the epic); cuneiform on clay tablets Oldest copy Old Babylonian epic tablets (e.g. the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets); the fullest version from Nineveh, c. 1800-1700 BCE; Nineveh copies 7th c. BCE Where it is now Penn Museum, Yale Babylonian Collection; British Museum (Nineveh tablets) Size About 3,000 lines on 12 tablets in the Standard Babylonian version, with gaps still being filled Dating confidence medium What it says Gilgamesh, a bullying king of Uruk, meets his match in Enkidu, a wild man the gods create to keep him busy. They become best friends, kill the forest guardian Humbaba, snub the goddess Ishtar and slay her Bull of Heaven. The gods punish them: Enkidu dies. Terrified of death, Gilgamesh travels to Utnapishtim, survivor of a great flood, seeking immortality. He finds a plant of youth, and a snake steals it. He goes home and admires his city's walls instead. History check A Gilgamesh of Uruk appears in the Sumerian King List (with an impossible 126-year reign), and one of his legendary rivals, Enmebaragesi of Kish, is attested in his own inscriptions, so a real king around 2700 BCE is plausible. No inscription of Gilgamesh himself has been found. Uruk's huge walls are real. The flood episode borrows from the older Atrahasis story; Mesopotamian flood layers are local and of different dates. History check Mixed record Bus

chunks.heading: Enuma Elish
chunks.text: Babylonia Enuma Elish Debated, c. 1800-1100 BCE; many favour the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I (c. 1125-1104 BCE) Mixed record. Babylonia Enuma Elish Debated, c. 1800-1100 BCE; many favour the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I (c. 1125-1104 BCE) Mixed record Language and script Akkadian (Standard Babylonian); cuneiform on clay Oldest copy Tablet copies from Ashur, Kish and the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, 1st millennium BCE (earliest c. 9th c. BCE) Where it is now British Museum and other collections Size About 1,100 lines on 7 tablets Dating confidence low-medium What it says Before sky and earth had names, sweet water (Apsu) and salt water (Tiamat) mingled. Their divine children are so noisy that Apsu plots to kill them; the clever god Ea strikes first. Furious, Tiamat raises an army of monsters. Young Marduk agrees to fight only if crowned king of the gods. He blasts her with winds, splits her body like a dried fish to make sky and earth, creates humans from a rebel god's blood to do the gods' chores, and builds Babylon. History check As an account of creation it is myth. As political history it fits well: it celebrates Marduk's rise to the top of the pantheon, which tracks Babylon's own rise.
