Later ritual texts indicate it was recited during the Akitu New Year festival. Its exact date of composition is still argued. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Mythic cosmology; reliable mirror of Babylonian politics and religion. The title just means 'When on high', the poem's first two words. The last tablet is a victory list of Marduk's 50 names.

chunks.heading: The Instruction of Ptahhotep
chunks.text: Middle Kingdom Egypt (set in the Old Kingdom) The Instruction of Ptahhotep Set in the reign of Djedkare Isesi (c. 2400 BCE); language suggests composition c. 2000-1800 BCE Plausible. Middle Kingdom Egypt (set in the Old Kingdom) The Instruction of Ptahhotep Set in the reign of Djedkare Isesi (c. 2400 BCE); language suggests composition c. 2000-1800 BCE Plausible Language and script Middle Egyptian; hieratic script on papyrus Oldest copy Papyrus Prisse, c. 1800 BCE (12th Dynasty) Where it is now Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris Size 37 maxims plus a prologue and epilogue Dating confidence low for the attribution, medium for Middle Kingdom composition What it says An aging vizier asks the king to let him train his son, and opens with a grumpy list of what old age does to the body. Then comes the advice: stay humble, because 'good speech is more hidden than greenstone, yet it is found among the women at the grindstones'. Listen more than you talk. Do not gossip. Do not grab food at a superior's table. Be generous, love your wife, and do not let success make you arrogant. Some tips would suit a modern office. History check King Djedkare Isesi and viziers named Ptahhotep are attested, including tombs at Saqqara. But the grammar and style point to the Middle Kingdom, so the attribution is probably a literary device giving the text an ancient pedigree. History check Plausible Busted Rock solid Real names and setting; authorship probably later than claimed. Papyrus Prisse, acquired in Egypt in the 1840s by Émile Prisse d'Avennes, is often nicknamed 'the oldest book in the world'.

chunks.heading: Code of Hammurabi
chunks.text: Old Babylonian Mesopotamia Code of Hammurabi c. 1755-1750 BCE, late in Hammurabi's reign (c. 1792-1750 BCE, middle chronology) Rock solid. Old Babylonian Mesopotamia Code of Hammurabi c. 1755-1750 BCE, late in Hammurabi's reign (c. 1792-1750 BCE, middle chronology) Rock solid Language and script Akkadian; cuneiform carved on a basalt stele Oldest copy The 2.25 m black stone stele, c. 1754 BCE Where it is now Louvre, Paris (found at Susa, Iran, in 1901-02) Size Prologue, 282 laws (as numbered by modern scholars), epilogue Dating confidence high relative date; absolute date depends on the chronology used What it says A king announces that the gods chose him 'to make justice appear in the land' and protect the weak from the strong. Then come the case rulings: theft, trade, wages, rent, marriage, divorce, adoption, surgeons' fees and building collapses. 'An eye for an eye' applies, but only between social equals; hurting a commoner or a slave costs silver instead. If a house falls and kills its owner, the builder dies. It is justice, Bronze Age style. History check Hammurabi is one of the best-attested kings of antiquity: his letters, year names, contracts and many tablet copies of the laws survive. Scholars debate whether courts actually applied the code; few trial records cite it, so it may have worked as royal showcase and model rulings. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid The king, the text and its date are firmly attested; everyday legal use is debated. The stele was itself war loot: an Elamite king, Shutruk-Nahhunte, carried it to Susa in the 12th century BCE, and several columns were chiselled off, perhaps for a boast he never carved.

chunks.heading: Rigveda
chunks.text: Vedic Indo-Aryans, northwestern Indian subcontinent Rigveda c. 1500-1000 BCE (older hymns c. 1500-1200 BCE) Plausible. Vedic Indo-Aryans, northwestern Indian subcontinent Rigveda c. 1500-1000 BCE (older hymns c. 1500-1200 BCE) Plausible Language and script Vedic Sanskrit; transmitted orally, later written in scripts such as Sharada and Devanagari Oldest copy Manuscripts in the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute collection (UNESCO Memory of the World, 2007), Oldest dated: 1464 CE Where it is now BORI, Pune, India Size 10 books (mandalas), 1,028 hymns, about 10,600 verses Dating confidence medium; based on linguistics and external anchors What it says A collection of hymns sung at fire rituals. Agni, the fire, carries offerings to the gods. Indra, a thunder-wielding hero fuelled by the drink soma, slays the serpent Vritra and frees the rivers. Ushas, the dawn, is praised in some of its loveliest poems, and Varuna guards cosmic order. One late hymn wonders how creation began and ends with a shrug: perhaps even the highest overseer 'knows, or perhaps he does not know'. History check The hymns describe a mobile, cattle-herding society with horses and chariots, and their river names fit the Punjab region. A Hittite-Mitanni treaty of about 1380 BCE invokes Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas, an independent sign these gods were known by the 14th century BCE. Exact dates and the question of origins remain debated. History check Plausible Busted Rock solid Reliable window on an early society; dating is approximate. The text was preserved by memory for many centuries using cross-checking recitation patterns (pada, krama, jata, ghana) that make errors easy to spot. Vedic chanting is on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

chunks.heading: Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day)
chunks.text: New Kingdom to Ptolemaic Egypt Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day) Emerges c. 1700-1550 BCE from earlier Coffin Texts; used until c. 50 BCE Rock solid. New Kingdom to Ptolemaic Egypt Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day) Emerges c. 1700-1550 BCE from earlier Coffin Texts; used until c. 50 BCE Rock solid Language and script Egyptian; hieroglyphic and hieratic on papyrus, coffins and shrouds Oldest copy Early spells on the coffin of Queen Mentuhotep (13th Dynasty); the famous Papyrus of Ani, c. 1700 BCE; Ani c. 1250 BCE Where it is now Coffin now lost (known from copies); Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum Size About 190 spells known; no single copy has them all. The Papyrus of Ani is over 20 m long Dating confidence high What it says A personalized survival kit for the afterlife. Spells let the dead transform into a heron or a lotus, avoid walking upside down, and keep their heart in place. The big moment is spell 125: in the Hall of Two Truths the heart is weighed against the feather of Maat while the deceased recites a 'negative confession': I have not stolen, I have not lied. Fail, and the monster Ammit, part crocodile, part lion, part hippo, eats the heart. History check Thousands of copies come from dated tombs, so the text's use and development are very well documented. It records what elite Egyptians hoped for after death rather than events. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid As evidence of Egyptian funerary belief and practice. Some copies were prepared in advance with blank spaces where the buyer's name would be filled in later: a ready-made afterlife guide.

chunks.heading: Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), including the Torah
chunks.text: Ancient Israel and Judah; Jewish communities of the Persian and Hellenistic eras Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), including the Torah Written and edited over c. 9th/8th-2nd c. BCE; the Torah probably reached its present form c. 6th-5th c. BCE Mixed record. Ancient Israel and Judah; Jewish communities of the Persian and Hellenistic eras Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), including the Torah Written and edited over c. 9th/8th-2nd c. BCE; the Torah probably reached its present form c. 6th-5th c. BCE Mixed record Language and script Biblical Hebrew with some Aramaic; Paleo-Hebrew, later Aramaic square script Oldest copy Ketef Hinnom silver amulets (the Priestly Blessing, Numbers 6:24-26); oldest complete Hebrew Bible: Leningrad Codex, Amulets c. 600 BCE; Leningrad Codex 1008 CE Where it is now Israel Museum, Jerusalem; National Library of Russia, St Petersburg Size 24 books in the Jewish count; the Torah alone is about 80,000 Hebrew words Dating confidence low-medium; actively debated What it says A library rather than a book: creation, a flood, the families of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Exodus from Egypt and laws given at Sinai, then settlement, judges, kings, prophets, exile to Babylon and return. Alongside the stories sit poetry (Psalms, Song of Songs), proverbs, the long argument of Job and the gloriously skeptical Ecclesiastes. It is history, law, poetry and argument woven together by many hands. History check Independent inscriptions confirm several figures and events: the Tel Dan stele mentions the 'House of David', the Mesha stele names Omri of Israel, Assyrian records name Jehu and Hezekiah, and Babylonian ration tablets list King Jehoiachin. The patriarchs, the Exodus and a sweeping conquest lack direct archaeological support, and the scale of the early monarchy is debated. History

chunks.heading: Iliad and Odyssey
chunks.text: Archaic Greece Iliad and Odyssey c. 750-650 BCE, from a much older oral tradition; fixed in writing between the 8th and 6th c. BCE Plausible. Archaic Greece Iliad and Odyssey c. 750-650 BCE, from a much older oral tradition; fixed in writing between the 8th and 6th c. BCE Plausible Language and script Homeric Greek (an artificial poetic mix of dialects); Greek alphabet Oldest copy Papyrus fragments from Egypt; oldest complete Iliad manuscript: Venetus A, Fragments from 3rd c. BCE; Venetus A 10th c. CE Where it is now Various papyrus collections; Biblioteca Marciana, Venice Size Iliad 15,693 lines; Odyssey 12,109 lines Dating confidence medium What it says The Iliad covers a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War: Achilles sulks after an insult, his friend Patroclus is killed, Achilles kills Hector in revenge, and old King Priam sneaks into the enemy camp to beg for his son's body. The Odyssey follows Odysseus's ten-year trip home past a Cyclops, the witch Circe, the Sirens and the land of the dead, ending with a bow contest and a hall full of doomed suitors. History check Troy is identified with Hisarlik in Turkey, a real city destroyed more than once around 1300-1180 BCE. Hittite texts mention Wilusa (likely Ilios), a king called Alaksandu and a western power called Ahhiyawa (likely Achaeans). The boar's-tusk helmet in the Iliad matches Mycenaean finds. The heroes, gods and a single ten-year war remain unattested. History check Plausible Busted Rock solid A real Bronze Age setting with a possible kernel of conflict, heavily legendary. There is no Trojan Horse in the Iliad. It appears only as a memory in the Odyssey (books 4 and 8), and the full tale is told much later by Virgil.

chunks.heading: Avesta
chunks.text: Ancient Iranian peoples; Zoroastrian tradition Avesta Gathas perhaps c. 1500-1000 BCE (proposals range to c. 500 BCE); Young Avestan texts later; written down in Sasanian times Hot debate. Ancient Iranian peoples; Zoroastrian tradition Avesta Gathas perhaps c. 1500-1000 BCE (proposals range to c. 500 BCE); Young Avestan texts later; written down in Sasanian times Hot debate Language and script Avestan (Old and Young Avestan); written in the Avestan alphabet, invented c. 5th-6th c. CE Oldest copy Manuscripts J2 and L4, the oldest securely dated, 1323 CE Where it is now UK libraries (Oxford and London); over 300 Avestan manuscripts are known Size About 83,000 surviving words, perhaps a quarter of the Sasanian-era Avesta Dating confidence low What it says At its heart are the Gathas, 17 hymns attributed to the prophet Zarathustra, who talks directly with the wise lord Ahura Mazda. The big theme is choice: every person sides with truth (asha) or with the lie (druj). Around the Gathas sit liturgies for the fire ritual, hymns to divine beings such as Mithra and Anahita, and the Vendidad, a rulebook on purity, dogs, and how to keep the dead from polluting earth, fire and water. History check The Gathas' language is very close to Rigvedic Sanskrit, which supports an early date. Achaemenid inscriptions of Darius I (c. 520 BCE) invoke Ahuramazda, so the god was central by then. Zarathustra himself has no external attestation, and his date is one of the most contested in the history of religion. History check Hot debate Busted Rock solid The tradition is ancient; the founder's date and life are uncertain. The Avestan alphabet, with more than 50 letters, was invented centuries after the texts were composed, largely to record pronunciation precisely as priests chanted it.

chunks.heading: Shijing (Classic of Poetry)
chunks.text: Zhou dynasty China Shijing (Classic of Poetry) c. 1000-600 BCE Strong. Zhou dynasty China Shijing (Classic of Poetry) c. 1000-600 BCE Strong Language and script Old Chinese; Chinese characters on bamboo and silk Oldest copy Warring States bamboo slips held by Anhui University; Han-era Fuyang slips, c. 4th c. BCE; Fuyang c. 165 BCE Where it is now Anhui University, Hefei; Fuyang material in Anhui Size 305 poems Dating confidence medium-high What it says China's oldest poetry anthology. The 'Airs of the States' are folk songs about love, flirting by the river, harvests, homesick soldiers and brides leaving home. One poem begs a 'big rat' to stop eating the grain: a thinly veiled complaint about greedy lords. The court odes and temple hymns praise Zhou ancestors such as King Wen and King Wu, who overthrew the Shang. It is sung history and everyday feeling in one. History check Kings and events named in the hymns match Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, including the Zhou conquest of the Shang (c. 1046 BCE). Bamboo manuscripts from the 4th century BCE show the poems circulated before the Qin book burning, with variant wording. History check Strong Busted Rock solid Names and institutions largely match bronze-age inscriptions. Tradition says Confucius picked these 305 from about 3,000 poems; most scholars doubt it. He did tell his son that without studying the Odes, 'you will have nothing to say'.

chunks.heading: Analects of Confucius (Lunyu)
chunks.text: Lu state, Spring and Autumn to Han China Analects of Confucius (Lunyu) Compiled by disciples and later followers, c. 5th-3rd c. BCE, taking final shape by the Han Strong. Lu state, Spring and Autumn to Han China Analects of Confucius (Lunyu) Compiled by disciples and later followers, c. 5th-3rd c. BCE, taking final shape by the Han Strong Language and script Classical Chinese; Chinese characters on bamboo slips Oldest copy Dingzhou bamboo slips; Haihun marquis tomb slips, Before 55 BCE (Dingzhou) and 59 BCE (Haihun) Where it is now Hebei and Jiangxi provinces, China Size 20 books, about 500 short passages, roughly 16,000 characters Dating confidence medium What it says Short sayings and scenes starring a teacher and his students. 'Is it not a pleasure to learn and practice what you have learned?' opens the book. Confucius praises humaneness (ren), ritual (li) and the gentleman who does not impose on others what he would not want himself. He can be funny and exasperated too: catching a student napping in the daytime, he says rotten wood cannot be carved. History check Confucius (traditionally 551-479 BCE) is widely accepted as historical, and other early texts mention him and his disciples. But the Analects was assembled in layers over generations, so individual sayings are hard to pin on him directly. History check Strong Busted Rock solid Historical teacher; the exact words are layered. The tomb of Liu He, Marquis of Haihun (d. 59 BCE), yielded slips that may belong to the lost 'Qi' version of the Analects, including a chapter title unseen for nearly 2,000 years.

chunks.heading: Tao Te Ching (Daodejing)
chunks.text: Warring States China Tao Te Ching (Daodejing) c. 4th c. BCE (with older sayings); traditionally attributed to Laozi, 6th c. BCE Hot debate. Warring States China Tao Te Ching (Daodejing) c. 4th c. BCE (with older sayings); traditionally attributed to Laozi, 6th c. BCE Hot debate Language and script Classical Chinese; bamboo slips and silk Oldest copy Guodian bamboo slips (partial); Mawangdui silk manuscripts (complete), c. 300 BCE; c. 168 BCE Where it is now Hubei Provincial Museum; Hunan Museum Size About 5,000 characters in 81 short chapters Dating confidence low for author, medium for dating What it says A tiny book of big paradoxes. 'The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao.' Water is soft yet wears down stone, so yielding beats forcing. The wise ruler practises wu wei, acting without straining, and governs a great state 'like cooking a small fish': do not poke it too much. It praises simplicity, humility and knowing when enough is enough, and it makes fun of cleverness and showy virtue. History check Laozi's biography comes from Sima Qian (c. 94 BCE), who himself offered several candidates. The Guodian slips show that sections of the text existed by about 300 BCE, but not necessarily as one book by one author. History check Hot debate Busted Rock solid The text is ancient; its author may be legendary. The Mawangdui silk copies put the 'Te' half first, so the oldest complete versions are really the Te Tao Ching.

chunks.heading: Pali Canon (Tipitaka)
chunks.text: Theravada Buddhist tradition, South and Southeast Asia Pali Canon (Tipitaka) Oral teachings from c. 5th c. BCE; written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st c. BCE Strong. Theravada Buddhist tradition, South and Southeast Asia Pali Canon (Tipitaka) Oral teachings from c. 5th c. BCE; written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st c. BCE Strong Language and script Pali; written in Sinhala, Burmese, Khmer, Thai, Pyu and later Roman scripts Oldest copy The Pyu 'golden Pali text': 20 gold leaves, c. 5th-6th c. CE Where it is now Found at Sri Ksetra, Myanmar Size Three 'baskets' (discipline, discourses, higher teaching); dozens of volumes in printed editions Dating confidence medium What it says The Vinaya sets rules for monks and nuns, and often explains each rule with the story of the monk whose mishap caused it. The Suttas hold the Buddha's talks: the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, and parables like the raft you leave behind once you have crossed the river, or blind men arguing over what an elephant is. The Abhidhamma breaks the mind into moments and parts like an early psychology manual. History check Ashoka's inscriptions (3rd c. BCE) mention the Buddha, and the Lumbini pillar states that the Buddha was born there. The Buddha's own dates remain debated (c. 563-483 or c. 480-400 BCE). The oldest Buddhist manuscripts of all are Gandharan birch-bark scrolls in the Gandhari language, not Pali. History check Strong Busted Rock solid Historical teacher and early community; wording shaped by centuries of oral transmission. Sri Lankan chronicles say monks wrote the canon down at Aluvihare cave after famine and war threatened the people who held it in memory.

chunks.heading: Mahabharata
chunks.text: Ancient India Mahabharata c. 400 BCE-400 CE, in layers Hot debate. Ancient India Mahabharata c. 400 BCE-400 CE, in layers Hot debate Language and script Sanskrit; transmitted orally and in many scripts Oldest copy Spitzer Manuscript fragment listing the epic's books; complete manuscripts much later, Spitzer c. 2nd c. CE; full manuscripts from the 2nd millennium CE Where it is now Spitzer fragments from Kizil, Xinjiang; full manuscripts in Indian and Nepalese collections Size About 100,000 couplets in the traditional count; roughly seven times the Iliad and Odyssey combined by lines Dating confidence medium What it says A family feud that becomes a world war. The five Pandava brothers lose their kingdom and their shared wife Draupadi's dignity in a rigged dice game, survive 13 years of exile, then face their cousins the Kauravas in an 18-day battle at Kurukshetra. Just before the fighting, Krishna counsels the hesitant archer Arjuna: that dialogue is the Bhagavad Gita. The epic claims, with some justification, that what is here is found elsewhere, and what is not here is nowhere. History check The Kuru kingdom was real (Iron Age, c. 1200-500 BCE, associated with Painted Grey Ware culture), and excavations at Hastinapura found a settlement of that period. No archaeological trace of a great war has been found, and astronomical dates proposed for it (such as 3102 BCE) are disputed. History check Hot debate Busted Rock solid Real Iron Age polity; the war and heroes are unverified. In the frame story the sage Vyasa dictates the epic to the elephant-headed god Ganesha, who agrees to write only if Vyasa never pauses, and breaks off a tusk to use as a pen.

chunks.heading: Histories of Herodotus
chunks.text: Classical Greece (Herodotus of Halicarnassus) Histories of Herodotus c. 440-425 BCE Mixed record. Classical Greece (Herodotus of Halicarnassus) Histories of Herodotus c. 440-425 BCE Mixed record Language and script Ionic Greek; Greek alphabet Oldest copy Papyrus fragments from Oxyrhynchus; oldest complete manuscript Codex Laurentianus 70.3, Fragments 1st-3rd c. CE; codex 10th c. CE Where it is now Oxford and other papyrus collections; Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence Size 9 books; roughly 190,000 Greek words Dating confidence high What it says The first big 'inquiry' (historia) in Greek: why did Greeks and Persians go to war? Along the way Herodotus detours into everything. Egyptian crocodiles and mummification, Scythian steam baths, a singer rescued by a dolphin, King Croesus misreading an oracle, and Indian ants that dig up gold. Then the main event: Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis, told with a sharp eye for pride and its fall. History check Persian royal inscriptions and the Persepolis administrative tablets confirm many names and institutions; the Behistun inscription parallels his account of Darius's rise. Frozen Scythian tombs match some of the customs he describes. Some numbers are inflated, notably Xerxes' army of millions, and some stories are hearsay he admits he doubts. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Core events and many details corroborated; numbers and tall tales are not. Explorer Michel Peissel proposed that the gold-digging 'ants' were Himalayan marmots, whose burrows on one high plateau throw up gold dust.

chunks.heading: New Testament
chunks.text: Early Christian communities, eastern Roman Empire New Testament c. 50-120 CE (Paul's letters c. 50-60; Gospels c. 70-100) Mixed record. Early Christian communities, eastern Roman Empire New Testament c. 50-120 CE (Paul's letters c. 50-60; Gospels c. 70-100) Mixed record Language and script Koine Greek; Greek uncial script on papyrus and parchment Oldest copy Papyrus P52 (a few verses of John 18); oldest complete New Testament: Codex Sinaiticus, P52 c. 125-175 CE (dating debated); Sinaiticus mid-4th c. CE Where it is now John Rylands Library, Manchester; mostly British Library, London Size 27 books; about 138,000 Greek words Dating confidence medium-high What it says Four Gospels tell the life, teaching, death and reported resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth from different angles. Acts follows the early movement from Jerusalem to Rome. Then come letters, many by Paul, full of advice, theology and arguments with local congregations, and finally Revelation, a vivid apocalyptic vision packed with symbolic beasts and numbers. Its most famous passages, from the Sermon on the Mount to the parable of the Good Samaritan, still shape everyday language. History check Most historians accept that Jesus existed and was executed under Pontius Pilate; Tacitus and Josephus mention him. A 1961 inscription from Caesarea names Pilate as prefect of Judea. Some details are problematic, such as the census of Quirinius (6 CE) versus Herod's death (4 BCE). Miracle claims lie outside what historical method can test. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Setting and several figures corroborated; many events untestable. P52 is about the size of a credit card. More than 5,000 Greek manuscripts of the New Testament survive, more than for any other ancient text.

chunks.heading: Popol Vuh
chunks.text: K'iche' Maya, highland Guatemala Popol Vuh Written c. 1554-1558 CE from much older traditions Mixed record. K'iche' Maya, highland Guatemala Popol Vuh Written c. 1554-1558 CE from much older traditions Mixed record Language and script K'iche' Mayan written in the Latin alphabet Oldest copy Francisco Ximénez's manuscript, K'iche' and Spanish in parallel columns, c. 1701-1703 CE Where it is now Newberry Library, Chicago Size Four parts; roughly 8,000-9,000 lines in line-by-line translations Dating confidence high for the writing; older sources uncertain What it says The gods try to make people who will praise them. Mud people melt. Wooden people have no hearts, so their own dogs, pots and grinding stones rise up against them. Before humans are made from maize, the Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque play the ballgame against the lords of the underworld, Xibalba, survive the House of Razors and the House of Bats, outwit death, and rise as the sun and moon. Then comes the history of K'iche' lineages. History check Scenes of the Hero Twins and the maize god appear in Classic Maya art, and related maize-god imagery appears in the San Bartolo murals of about 100 BCE, showing these myths are far older than the manuscript. The later dynastic sections match other K'iche' documents and the ruins of their capital, Q'umarkaj. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Myths are ancient and corroborated in art; late dynastic history reasonably supported. The original K'iche' manuscript is lost. The text survived only because a Dominican friar copied it around 1701; the copy resurfaced in Guatemala in the 1850s and now sits in Chicago.

chunks.heading: Quran
chunks.text: 7th-century Arabia Quran 610-632 CE (traditional period of revelation); compiled as a standard codex c. 650 CE by tradition Mixed record. 7th-century Arabia Quran 610-632 CE (traditional period of revelation); compiled as a standard codex c. 650 CE by tradition Mixed record Language and script Classical Arabic; early Hijazi script, later Kufic Oldest copy The Birmingham leaves (two parchment folios); other early witnesses include the Sanaa palimpsest, Parchment radiocarbon-dated to 568-645 CE (95% probability) Where it is now Cadbury Research Library, University of Birmingham (Mingana Collection) Size 114 suras, 6,236 verses (common count), about 77,000 words Dating confidence high for an early date, supported by manuscript evidence What it says Arabic scripture presented as recited revelation. Its themes include one God, gratitude, justice, care for orphans and the poor, and a coming day of judgement. It retells stories of figures shared with Jewish and Christian traditions, such as Abraham, Moses, Mary and Jesus, often briefly and with a moral point, and it gives guidance on law and community life. It is famous for rhythmic rhymed prose meant to be heard aloud. History check Radiocarbon dates on early parchments (Birmingham, Tubingen, Sanaa) support a written text very early, consistent with a 7th-century origin. Its references to ancient figures overlap with biblical traditions and are largely beyond archaeological testing, as with other scriptures. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Early textual history well supported; ancient narratives largely untestable. The Birmingham leaves sat in a university collection for about 90 years before a researcher's close look led to radiocarbon testing in 2015.

chunks.heading: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters)
chunks.text: Nara-period Japan Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters) Presented to the court in 712 CE Mixed record. Nara-period Japan Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters) Presented to the court in 712 CE Mixed record Language and script Old Japanese written with Chinese characters, partly as Chinese prose and partly phonetically Oldest copy Shinpukuji manuscript, copied by the monk Ken'yu (a National Treasure), 1371-1372 CE Where it is now Shinpukuji temple (Osu Kannon), Nagoya Size 3 volumes Dating confidence high What it says Two gods, Izanagi and Izanami, stir the ocean with a jeweled spear, and the drips form the islands of Japan. Izanami dies giving birth to fire, and Izanagi follows her to the land of the dead, then flees in horror. The sun goddess Amaterasu hides in a cave and darkens the world until the gods throw a raucous party outside. Her brother Susanoo slays an eight-headed serpent and finds a sword in its tail. Then come the emperors. History check The first emperor Jimmu's traditional date (660 BCE) is not supported by archaeology, which shows the Yayoi and Kofun periods instead. Later reigns fit better: a 5th-century sword inscription from Inariyama names a king widely matched to Emperor Yuryaku. Chinese records mention a queen Himiko who does not appear in the Kojiki at all. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Mythic early chapters; later royal history partly corroborated. The compiler, O no Yasumaro, wrote down what the court reciter Hieda no Are had memorized. Yasumaro's own tomb and bronze epitaph were found in 1979 in a Nara tea field.

chunks.heading: Dead Sea Scrolls
chunks.text: Second Temple Judea Dead Sea Scrolls Copied c. 250 BCE-68 CE Rock solid. Second Temple Judea Dead Sea Scrolls Copied c. 250 BCE-68 CE Rock solid Language and script Hebrew, Aramaic and some Greek; mostly square Jewish script, some Paleo-Hebrew Oldest copy The scrolls are themselves the old copies; the Great Isaiah Scroll is the showpiece, Oldest fragments 3rd c. BCE; Great Isaiah Scroll c. 2nd c. BCE Where it is now Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem, and other collections Size About 900-1,000 manuscripts in tens of thousands of fragments from 11 caves near Qumran (found 1947-1956) Dating confidence high (handwriting study plus radiocarbon) What it says A library hidden in desert caves. It holds the oldest known copies of almost every book of the Hebrew Bible (Esther is missing), plus writings no one had seen for 2,000 years: rules for a strict community, a War Scroll about the 'Sons of Light' fighting the 'Sons of Darkness', hymns, calendars, commentaries, and the Copper Scroll, a list of hidden treasure engraved on metal. History check Radiocarbon tests and handwriting analysis agree on dates from about the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE; the nearby Qumran settlement was destroyed around 68 CE. The Isaiah scroll is remarkably close to the medieval text, while other books show variant versions, showing both careful copying and a still-fluid text. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid As direct evidence of how scriptures were copied and read in the Second Temple period. The first scrolls were found in 1946-47 by Bedouin shepherds, reportedly while looking for a stray goat. The Copper Scroll lists dozens of treasure caches; none has ever been found.

chunks.heading: Rosetta Stone
chunks.text: Ptolemaic Egypt Rosetta Stone 196 BCE (decree of priests at Memphis honouring Ptolemy V) Rock solid. Ptolemaic Egypt Rosetta Stone 196 BCE (decree of priests at Memphis honouring Ptolemy V) Rock solid Language and script Egyptian in hieroglyphic and Demotic scripts, plus Ancient Greek Oldest copy The granodiorite stele itself, about 760 kg, 196 BCE; found July 1799 at Rashid (Rosetta) Where it is now British Museum, London (since 1802) Size 14 surviving lines of hieroglyphs, 32 of Demotic, 54 of Greek Dating confidence high What it says Surprisingly, a piece of bureaucracy. Priests thank the young king Ptolemy V for tax breaks, gifts to temples and crushing a rebellion, and in return vote him statues and festivals. The key line orders the decree to be set up in every major temple in 'sacred', 'native' and Greek writing. That last detail made it the key: one message in three scripts, one of which scholars could already read. History check Other copies of the same decree have been found, and its events match the known reign of Ptolemy V. Using the Greek as a guide, Thomas Young made early progress and Jean-François Champollion announced the decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid An official dated document; its account of a royal decree is corroborated. Legend says Champollion ran into his brother's office shouting 'Je tiens l'affaire!' ('I've got it!') and then fainted.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu
chunks.text: Giza, Egypt The Great Pyramid of Khufu 11 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read c. 146.6 m original height, the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years Petrie 1883; Lehner 1997 c. 2,300,000 blocks estimated stone blocks Lehner 1997 c. 40 boatmen in Merer's crew, shipping Tura limestone Tallet 2017 c. 64 km length of the buried Ahramat Nile branch beside the pyramid fields Ghoneim et al. 2024 ≥ 30 m minimum length of the Big Void found by muons Morishima et al. 2017 c. 20 cm largest difference between the four base sides Cole 1925 c. 146.6 m (now c. 138.5 m) Original height c. 230.3 m; the four sides differ by about 20 cm Base side c. 51.8° Slope c. 2.3 million (an estimate, not a count) Estimated blocks c. 6 million tonnes Estimated mass c. 40 boatmen; 2–3 round trips every 10 days Merer's crew at least 30 m long, above the Grand Gallery Big Void (2017) c. 9 m long, c. 2 x 2 m in section North Face Corridor (2023) The best evidence comes from the builders' own paperwork. Papyri found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, Egypt's oldest known harbour, include the logbook of an inspector named Merer, whose crew of about 40 men shipped white Tura limestone to Giza in Khufu's 27th year along canals into a harbour basin. A 2024 study mapped a buried Nile branch, the Ahramat, running past 31 pyramids, so boats could reach close to the building sites. Most core blocks were quarried on the plateau itself, a short haul from the pyramid. Sledges dragged over wetted sand, levers, ropes and ramps are well attested. The exact layout of the ramps used for the upper courses is still debated, and so is how the heaviest granite beams were lifted about 43 m to the King's Chamber. The myth The pyramid is too precise for Bronze Age tools, and satellite radar has revealed a hidde

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 01 A diary from the building site
chunks.text: In 2013, in a cave gallery on the Red Sea coast at Wadi al-Jarf, a French and Egyptian team led by Pierre Tallet lifted out bundles of papyrus that had been sealed away for about 4,500 years. Some were accounts. The best preserved were a logbook kept by an inspector called Merer, who ran a crew of roughly 40 boatmen in the 27th year of King Khufu. Day after day, in tidy columns, Merer noted where the crew slept, where they loaded, and where they delivered. What they carried was fine white limestone from the quarries at Tura, across the river from Giza. What they delivered it to was Akhet Khufu, 'Horizon of Khufu', the name of the king's pyramid. The entries mention a harbour basin and a stop called She-Khufu, and they name Khufu's half-brother Ankhhaf as the senior official in charge of the work. By Tallet's reading, the crew made two or three round trips about every ten days. The oldest inscribed papyri we have are not hymns or laws. They are a boatman's timesheets from the Great Pyramid. That is the right place to start, because the Great Pyramid is often presented as a riddle with no witnesses. It has witnesses. They were paid in bread and beer, and at least one of them kept a diary.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 02 A mountain, measured
chunks.text: When Flinders Petrie surveyed Giza between 1880 and 1882, he treated the pyramid like a laboratory instrument. His numbers, refined by J. H. Cole's survey of 1925, still frame everything: a square base about 230.3 m on a side, an original height of about 146.6 m, and faces rising at about 51.8°. The four sides differ in length by only about 20 cm, and they are aligned to the cardinal points to within a few arcminutes. Today the top 8 m or so are missing and the height is about 138.5 m. The volume is about 2.6 million cubic metres. Divide by a typical block and you get the famous figure of about 2.3 million blocks, with a total mass near 6 million tonnes. Treat both as engineering estimates rather than counts: nobody has tallied the blocks, the core contains rubble and uneven fill, and the granite beams over the King's Chamber are far heavier than the average core block of a tonne or two. How did they find north so precisely without a compass? Several methods would work. Egyptologist Kate Spence proposed in 2000 that surveyors waited for two circumpolar stars to line up vertically, then dropped a plumb line; because the stars drift slowly over centuries, her idea also offered a way to date the pyramids. Others have shown that simple sun-shadow methods, tracking the tip of a vertical rod through a day, can reach similar accuracy. Nobody knows which one Khufu's surveyors used, but none requires anything more exotic than patience, cord and a clear sky. For about 3,800 years it was the tallest thing people had built, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England rose higher around 1311 CE. It was already an antique, more than 2,000 years old, when Greek writers put it on their list of wonders. The capstone and the top courses are gone, so the original apex is reconstructed

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 03 Inside the mountain
chunks.text: The interior is surprisingly small: a few narrow passages and three main chambers inside six million tonnes of stone. The original entrance sits about 17 m up the north face. From it a passage runs down at about 26.5° through the masonry and into the bedrock, ending in a rough, unfinished chamber about 30 m below the base. Partway down, an ascending passage branches upward, once blocked by granite plugs, and opens into the Grand Gallery, a corbelled hall about 46.7 m long and 8.6 m high. Scale cross-section of the Great Pyramid, north on the left. From an entrance about 17 m up the north face, the descending passage runs down at 26.5 degrees into bedrock to an unfinished subterranean chamber about 30 m below the base. The ascending passage rises to the Grand Gallery, 46.7 m long and 8.6 m high. A level passage leads to the Queen's Chamber on the midline. At the top of the gallery is the granite King's Chamber, about 43 m up, with five relieving chambers above. Two shafts from the King's Chamber reach the faces; two from the Queen's Chamber end at stone doors. A dashed red band above the gallery marks the Big Void, and a small one behind the entrance marks the North Face Corridor. Scale bar 50 m; base 230.3 m; original height 146.6 m. A level passage leads from the foot of the gallery to the so-called Queen's Chamber, sitting exactly on the pyramid's north to south midline. At the top of the gallery lies the King's Chamber, lined with Aswan granite and holding an empty lidless granite sarcophagus. Above it, five low compartments separated by huge granite beams, the 'relieving chambers', spread the weight of the masonry overhead. Workers' graffiti painted inside them include Khufu's name, one of the direct links between the monument and its king. Four narrow shafts compli

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 04 Merer's river road
chunks.text: Merer's logbook turns a mystery of logistics into a timetable. Casing stone was loaded at Tura, floated across the Nile and along a canal, and delivered to a harbour near the building site. Each round trip took about four days. Tallet estimates each boat carried about 30 blocks of 2 to 3 tonnes, on the order of 200 blocks a month for one crew. Granite for the King's Chamber came from Aswan, more than 900 km upstream by river, and would have travelled the same way. In 2024 a team led by Eman Ghoneim added the missing landscape. Using radar satellite imagery, geophysical surveys and deep sediment cores, they traced a buried branch of the Nile, which they named the Ahramat ('pyramids') branch, about 64 km long and 200 to 700 m wide, running along the desert edge from Lisht to Giza. Thirty-one pyramids, built over about a thousand years, line its banks, and many causeways end at valley temples that would have stood near its water. The pyramids were not built in the middle of nowhere. They were built on a waterfront that has since dried up and disappeared under fields and sand. The Ahramat study does not settle every detail. Water levels changed from season to season and from century to century, and the exact course of the channel in Khufu's reign is still being refined. But together with Merer's harbour basin it fits a simple, practical picture: move heavy stone by water whenever you can, and drag it only for the last stretch.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 05 From quarry to course
chunks.text: Most of the pyramid did not travel far at all. The core blocks were cut from quarries on the Giza plateau itself, just south of the pyramid, where the cut faces and the channels left around half-freed blocks are still visible. Quarrymen used copper chisels, stone pounders and wooden levers to separate blocks along their natural beds. Step 1 of 5. Quarry: most core blocks were cut from the plateau just south of the pyramid, separated by trenches and levered free. Quarry: most core blocks were cut from the plateau just south of the pyramid, separated by trenches and levered free. Sledge on wet sand: water poured ahead of the sledge stiffens the sand; experiments show it can roughly halve the pull. Boats and canal: Merer's crew brought white Tura limestone across the Nile to a harbour basin at the foot of the plateau. Ramps: blocks went up ramps against the growing pyramid. Their layout (straight, zigzag or wrapping) is still debated. Casing: fine white limestone was dressed smooth, probably from the top down as the ramps came away. Schematic landscape in five steps. Step 1: a stepped quarry pit cut into the Giza plateau, with a block freed by trenches and a worker with a lever. Step 2: a block on a wooden sledge dragged by a team with ropes while a man pours water on the sand ahead. Step 3: a boat carrying white casing blocks in a canal and harbour basin below the plateau. Step 4: a ramp zigzagging up the face of the half-built pyramid with a block on it. Step 5: the finished pyramid with its smooth white casing and capstone. Blocks were dragged on wooden sledges. A Middle Kingdom tomb painting of the official Djehutihotep shows a colossal statue on a sledge with a man pouring water onto the sand in front of it. In 2014 physicists at the University of Amsterdam tested why

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 06 The people who built it
chunks.text: About 400 m south of the Sphinx, beyond a massive stone boundary wall about 200 m long known as the Wall of the Crow, archaeologists led by Mark Lehner have excavated a planned settlement called Heit el-Ghurab since 1988. It has long galleries that may have housed rotating work gangs, bakeries with bread moulds, storerooms, and a large administrative building. Seal impressions date most of it to Khufu's successors Khafre and Menkaure, so it tells us how the Giza project was run in general, even if Khufu's own camp is less well preserved. The menu was generous. Zooarchaeologist Richard Redding's estimate, based on the animal bones, is that the town consumed on the order of 11 cattle and 37 sheep or goats a day, supplied by herds raised on estates in the Delta. On the slope above, Zahi Hawass's team found from 1990 the tombs of workers and overseers, with titles such as 'overseer of the side of the pyramid'. Some skeletons show healed fractures and even an amputation, signs of medical care. Of this oppression there passed ten years while the causeway was made by which they drew the stones ... For the making of the pyramid itself there passed a period of twenty years. Herodotus visited Egypt about 2,000 years after Khufu and repeated the local story that the king drove 100,000 men in three-month shifts. The idea that slaves built the pyramids comes mostly from later retellings. The archaeology points instead to a mixed workforce: a permanent core of skilled builders, supported by larger rotating crews drafted from the provinces, fed and housed by the state. Most published estimates of the number on site at any one time range from about 10,000 to 25,000.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 07 Seeing through stone
chunks.text: Every minute, each square metre of the Earth's surface is crossed by about ten thousand muons, heavy cousins of the electron made when cosmic rays hit the upper atmosphere. Stone absorbs some of them. Place detectors inside or beside a pyramid and count the muons arriving from each direction: where more get through than expected, there is less stone in the way, which means a void. The ScanPyramids project, launched in 2015 by Cairo University and the HIP Institute, used three independent detector technologies from Nagoya University, the Japanese laboratory KEK and the French agency CEA. In 2017 they reported in Nature a 'Big Void' above the Grand Gallery, at least 30 m long, with a cross-section similar to the gallery's. All three methods saw it. Its shape, slope and purpose are unknown; it could be one space or several. A second, smaller anomaly lay just behind the great limestone chevrons above the original entrance. In 2023 a paper in Nature Communications characterised this North Face Corridor as about 9 m long with a cross-section of about 2 by 2 m, and a thin endoscope pushed through a joint in the masonry showed a real, empty, gabled corridor. A 2025 study in Scientific Reports combined radar, ultrasound and electrical imaging to confirm its size and position. The North Face Corridor was photographed in February 2023 and independently confirmed by multi-method imaging in 2025. Most engineers suspect it helped relieve the load over the entrance, much as the chevrons do, but nobody has yet been inside it. The Big Void remains unvisited, and no drilling has been approved.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 08 Radar, a retraction and an underground city
chunks.text: Not every scan survives scrutiny. In 2022 Filippo Biondi and Corrado Malanga published a paper in the journal Remote Sensing claiming that a satellite radar technique had revealed undiscovered internal structures in the Great Pyramid. In 2025 the same researchers announced, at a press event rather than in a journal, far larger claims: vertical shafts and chambers reaching hundreds of metres beneath the neighbouring pyramid of Khafre. The story went viral as an 'underground city'. Specialists in ground-penetrating radar objected from the start. Radar at the frequencies used by these satellites is absorbed and scattered by the first metres of rock; archaeological radar expert Lawrence Conyers put it bluntly, saying it is physically impossible for the signal to pass through the pyramid, reflect off internal structures and return to the satellite. No raw data or peer-reviewed paper supported the Khafre claims. On 10 August 2026 Remote Sensing retracted the 2022 paper. The notice says an investigation by the editorial office and board 'confirmed serious methodological flaws and statistical errors that were deemed to undermine the scientific conclusions'. The authors disagreed with the decision. The retraction does not touch the muon results, which were produced by three independent teams using a method with a long record, from Luis Alvarez's scan of Khafre's pyramid in the 1960s to modern volcano imaging. A good anomaly survives a second team, a second method and a peer review. The Big Void did. The underground city did not.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: 09 What we still do not know
chunks.text: The broad story is well supported: a 4th Dynasty king, a state that could feed and organise many thousands of workers, local quarries, river transport, sledges, levers and ramps. What remains open is the fine print. How the upper third was built: which ramp layout, or mix of ramps and lifting from the courses, carried blocks above about 100 m. How the granite beams of the King's Chamber, some estimated at 25 to 80 tonnes, were raised about 43 m or more. What the Big Void is: a second gallery, a construction space, a relieving structure, or several of these. Why the Queen's Chamber shafts were sealed with small pinned slabs, and what lies a few metres beyond them. How long it took. Herodotus's twenty years and the length of Khufu's reign make a range of about 20 to 27 years plausible, but there is no direct record of the start date. The honest mystery rating is low, around 2 out of 5. The pyramid is astonishing, but its builders left their tools, their towns, their graves, their graffiti and their paperwork. Every new instrument has so far made the human story more detailed, not less likely.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: debate
chunks.text: Did satellite radar reveal hidden structures inside and beneath the Giza pyramids? Yes: the radar images show shafts, corridors and chambers far larger than the known interior. Biondi and Malanga 2022 (Remote Sensing) and their 2025 press announcement about Khafre's pyramid. No: the method cannot see that deep, and the published analysis failed review. Radar at these frequencies is absorbed within the first metres of rock; the 2022 paper was retracted in August 2026 for methodological flaws and statistical errors; the 2025 claims were never peer reviewed. The bold claim: Satellite radar has revealed a hidden complex of shafts and chambers inside and beneath the Giza pyramids. Receipt Meter Busted Busted Rock solid The one peer-reviewed paper behind the claim has been retracted by its journal after an investigation, and the larger claims were never submitted to review or released as data. The physics is also against it: satellite radar does not penetrate hundreds of metres of limestone. The real voids detected inside the pyramid come from muon imaging, a different method confirmed by three teams.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: debate
chunks.text: How were the upper courses built? External ramps: straight, zigzagging up a face, or wrapping around the pyramid. Ramp remains at other pyramids and quarries, including the Khufu-era Hatnub ramp with staircases and post holes; the practical need for access to every course. An internal spiral ramp inside the pyramid, proposed by Jean-Pierre Houdin. A notch high on one edge and microgravity data interpreted by Houdin; no internal ramp has been seen in muon scans so far. The bold claim: Khufu's builders raised the top of the pyramid using an internal spiral ramp. Receipt Meter No receipts yet Busted Rock solid External ramps of various layouts are attested in Egyptian building, and some combination of them remains the leading explanation, although the exact layout at Khufu's pyramid is unknown. The internal ramp idea is ingenious and testable, but the muon surveys that found the Big Void and the North Face Corridor have not reported the spiral it predicts.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu: debate
chunks.text: What is the Big Void? A construction feature: a relieving space, a second gallery used during building, or a void left by the building method. Its position above the Grand Gallery and its similar size and slope; the pyramid already has relieving chambers and chevrons. A hidden chamber, perhaps holding burial goods. The size of the void and the absence of any known access. The bold claim: The Big Void is a sealed treasure chamber. Receipt Meter No receipts yet Busted Rock solid The muon data show only that there is a large volume with less stone, at least 30 m long. They cannot show contents, and the physicists who found it stress that it may be several spaces and may be inclined or horizontal. A structural purpose linked to the Grand Gallery is the most economical guess, but only a camera or future imaging can decide.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe
chunks.text: Şanlıurfa, Türkiye Göbekli Tepe 11 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read c. 5.5 m height of the central pillars of Enclosure D DAI Göbekli Tepe project 11 pillars set into the ring wall of Enclosure D Haklay & Gopher 2020 c. 19.25 m side of the triangle linking the centres of Enclosures B, C and D Haklay & Gopher 2020 over 7,000 artefacts grinding stones and related tools analysed Dietrich L. et al. 2019 c. 300 m diameter of the artificial mound DAI Göbekli Tepe project c. 46 km to its sister site Karahan Tepe Karul 2021 built from c. 9600 BCE, abandoned c. 8000 BCE Age c. 5.5 m (P18 and P31, Enclosure D) Tallest pillars c. 8–10 t for the largest Pillar weight c. 14 m across inside, 11 pillars in the ring wall plus 2 central Enclosure D c. 300 m across, 15 m high, about 9 ha Mound a small fraction, roughly a tenth Excavated so far none Pottery, metal, writing The builders quarried hard limestone on the plateau beside the site, cutting T-shaped slabs out of bedrock with flint and stone tools; an unfinished pillar still lies in one quarry. Pillars were moved a short way, set into sockets or low pedestals, and linked by rubble walls and stone benches into round to oval enclosures. The biggest, Enclosure D, has two central pillars about 5.5 m tall and eleven more set into its ring wall. Reliefs of arms, hands, belts and fox-pelt loincloths turn the pillars into stylised human figures, surrounded by foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and scorpions. More than 7,000 grinding-stone artefacts show that cereals were processed on site in bulk, probably to feed work parties. Rainwater cisterns and domestic buildings suggest people also lived here. The myth A lost advanced civilisation built Göbekli Tepe, buried it on purpose to hide it, and carved a star map of a comet cat

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 01 A hill with a navel
chunks.text: Stand on the limestone ridge above the Harran plain on a spring morning and the wind carries the smell of wheat fields. Beneath a modern canopy, a ring of grey stone figures faces inwards towards two taller ones. They have no faces. They do have arms: long, bent arms carved in low relief down their sides, with hands whose fingers meet over the belly. Below the hands, a belt. Hanging from the belt, a fox pelt, tail down. These figures were raised around 11,500 years ago. That is roughly 7,000 years before the first Egyptian pyramid and more than 6,000 years before the first stones went up at Stonehenge. The people who raised them had no pottery, no metal, no writing and, as far as the animal bones show, no domesticated livestock. They hunted gazelle and wild cattle, and they harvested wild or barely domesticated cereals. The Turkish name, Göbekli Tepe, means roughly Potbelly Hill or Hill of the Navel. A 1963 survey by the Universities of Chicago and Istanbul noticed the mound and its broken limestone slabs, but took them for a medieval cemetery. In 1994 the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt looked again, recognised the T-shaped slabs as Stone Age pillars, and began excavating in 1995 with the German Archaeological Institute (DAI) and the Şanlıurfa Museum. Thirty years later, only a small fraction of the 300 m mound has been dug. Its builders had no pottery, no metal and no writing, yet they carved 5.5 m stone people with hands, belts and fox pelts.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 02 Rings of stone: Enclosures A to D
chunks.text: The famous part of the site is a cluster of big round to oval buildings that the excavators label with letters. Enclosures A, B, C and D sit in the main excavation area, and geophysical survey suggests more lie unexcavated in the mound. Each follows the same recipe: a wall of rubble stone, T-shaped pillars set into that wall at intervals with their narrow faces turned inwards, stone benches running between them, and a pair of larger pillars standing free in the middle. Enclosure D is the best preserved and the most spectacular. Its interior is about 14 m across at its widest, according to the architectural analysis by Gil Haklay and Avi Gopher. Eleven pillars stand in the ring wall. The central pair, known as Pillars 18 and 31, reach about 5.5 m and are thought to weigh around 8 to 10 tonnes each. They stand in low pedestals cut out of the bedrock, roughly 20 to 30 cm high. Plan view of an oval stone enclosure about 14 metres across inside. A thick rubble ring wall has a low bench along its inner face and eleven narrow rectangular pillars set into it, each pointing towards the centre. The pillar in the north-west, P43, the Vulture Stone, is highlighted. In the middle stand two pillars, P31 and P18, on low pedestals. A 5 metre scale bar and a north arrow are shown. An inset side view compares the 5.5 metre T-shaped Pillar 18 with a 1.7 metre person. Haklay and Gopher noticed something else. If you mark the centre points of Enclosures B, C and D on a plan, they form an almost perfect equilateral triangle with sides of about 19.25 m, accurate to within about 1.5 per cent. They argue that the three buildings were planned together as one project, perhaps laid out with cords and pegs. Not everyone agrees that the pattern was intended, but the precision is striking, and it hin

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 03 Stone people and a zoo of carvings
chunks.text: The T-shape is not decoration: it is a body. The horizontal top is a head seen from the side, and the shaft is a torso. On the two central pillars of Enclosure D, the carvers made this explicit. Arms run down the broad sides, bent at the elbow, and the hands meet on the front just above a belt. The belts carry symbols, and from each hangs a fox pelt, carved so clearly that the fur and tail are recognisable. Most researchers read the central pairs as supernatural beings or ancestors rather than portraits of individual people. Around these stone figures swarms an entire bestiary. Foxes leap across the shafts. Wild boars, snakes, cranes, vultures, aurochs, wild asses and scorpions appear in low and high relief. Snakes often flow downwards. The choice is not random: dangerous, carrion-eating or night-active animals dominate, and the domestic, the gentle and the edible are rare. Wild cattle and gazelle, which were eaten here in large numbers, appear far less often than foxes. Pillar 43 in Enclosure D, nicknamed the Vulture Stone, is the densest of all. On its upper front sits a large vulture with a circle beside one outstretched wing. Around it are smaller birds, a scorpion, a snake and, near the top, three rectangular objects with handles that visitors love to call handbags. At the bottom is a headless human figure with an erect phallus. Headless figures and carved human skulls at the site hint at a concern with the dead and with heads, a theme that returns at nearby sites.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 04 How to make a T-pillar
chunks.text: The raw material was right underfoot. The ridge is made of hard, flat-bedded limestone, and quarry traces on the plateau around the enclosures show where pillars were outlined, trenched and levered free. Schmidt described an unfinished pillar still lying in its bedrock bed, reported as around 7 m long. It shows the method: mark the outline, cut a channel around it with stone and flint tools, then split the slab off along a natural bedding plane. Step 1 of 5. Mark and trench: on the limestone plateau beside the site, workers outline a T-shaped slab and cut a channel around it with flint and stone tools. Mark and trench: on the limestone plateau beside the site, workers outline a T-shaped slab and cut a channel around it with flint and stone tools. Split it free: the rock's natural flat bedding helps. Wedges and wooden levers probably lifted the slab off its bed. Haul: the quarries lie on the same plateau, only a short way off, so ropes, rollers or sledges and many hands could move a pillar of up to about 10 t. Raise: the foot goes into a socket in a pedestal and the top is hauled upright with ropes and props. This is a proposed method, not a recorded one. Carve: arms, hands, belts and fox-pelt loincloths in low relief turn the pillar into a stylised figure. Some carving may have happened before raising. A strip drawing of the limestone plateau from quarry on the left to enclosure on the right. Step 1: a T-shaped outline is trenched into the bedrock by workers. Step 2: the slab is levered up along a bedding plane. Step 3: the pillar lies on wooden rollers and is pulled by people with ropes. Step 4: the pillar is tipped upright into a socket in a pedestal, with a prop and ropes. Step 5: the pillar stands upright with carved arm, belt and fox pelt while a person carves it.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 05 Not alone: the Stone Hills
chunks.text: For two decades Göbekli Tepe looked unique. It is not. Across the Şanlıurfa region, surveys and excavations now recognise a family of about a dozen contemporary sites with T-shaped pillars, grouped since 2021 under the name Taş Tepeler, the Stone Hills. Nevalı Çori, excavated in the 1980s and 1990s before a reservoir drowned it, had T-pillars with arms. Karahan Tepe, about 46 km to the east, may be even more startling. At Karahan Tepe, excavations led by Necmi Karul of Istanbul University since 2019 uncovered Structure AB, a room about 7 by 6 m cut partly into the bedrock. Ten of its eleven pillars were left standing out of the living rock as the room was carved around them, and they are shaped like phalluses. On the west wall, a human head with a beard and thick lips emerges from the rock, gazing towards the entrance steps. Next door, the larger Structure AD is about 23 m across. In 2023 the team also reported a seated human statue about 2.3 m tall with a V-shaped collar motif, echoing the famous Urfa Man statue found in the city in 1993. The effect of these finds is to turn Göbekli Tepe from a lonely miracle into the best-known member of a regional culture, with shared images, shared building habits and, perhaps, shared ceremonies.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 06 How old, exactly? The trouble with fill
chunks.text: Dating Göbekli Tepe is harder than it sounds. Radiocarbon needs something that was once alive: bone, charcoal, seeds. The enclosures, however, are full of debris, and debris moves. Material in the fill can be older than the building (if it was scraped up from an earlier rubbish layer) or younger (if it sifted in later). The DAI team has found cases of inverse stratigraphy, where younger samples lie deeper than older ones. The most direct dates come from organic material trapped in the wall plaster of the enclosures, since plaster was applied while the building was in use. One sample from Enclosure D gave 9984 ± 42 radiocarbon years, which calibrates to 9745–9314 cal BCE at 95 per cent probability. Charcoal from deep soundings in the same enclosure clusters between about 9660 and 9310 cal BCE. So Enclosure D was probably built and used in the mid to late 10th millennium BCE, and filled in later, in the 9th. The exact figures will keep moving as more samples are dated, and it is worth holding the headline number loosely. What is not in doubt is the order of magnitude: these buildings belong to the earliest Neolithic, the period when people in this region were starting to cultivate cereals but had not yet become full-time farmers.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 07 Buried on purpose? Maybe not
chunks.text: Klaus Schmidt, who died in 2014, believed the enclosures had been deliberately backfilled when they went out of use, a ritual burial that sealed them for millennia. The idea was elegant and it spread widely, including into claims that the site was hidden on purpose. After Schmidt's death, the team under Lee Clare re-examined the deposits. In a 2020 summary of the 2015–2019 work, Clare describes fill made of limestone rubble, flint and bone that seems to have slid into the buildings from higher knolls and slopes, mixing older and younger material. Moritz Kinzel and Clare argue that repeated slope slides damaged the enclosures during their use and that the builders repaired, reinforced and remodelled them. On this reading, the burial was gradual and partly accidental. There is a twist. At Karahan Tepe, Karul describes fill that stayed inside the building, went in by stages, and was capped with large flat stones, one measuring about 2.65 by 1.65 m. That looks intentional. So deliberate burial may have been a real practice in the Stone Hills, even if Göbekli Tepe's own enclosures were largely filled by nature and time.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 08 A temple on a hill, or a village?
chunks.text: Schmidt called Göbekli Tepe a mountain sanctuary, a place where scattered hunter-gatherer bands met for ceremonies and feasts but where nobody lived. The phrase "the world's first temple" still appears on posters. The newer evidence is less tidy and more interesting. Excavations since 2015 have found domestic buildings around the enclosures, first round to oval ones and, from about 8700 BCE, rectangular ones. They have found hearths, tool-making debris, the grinding stones mentioned above, and a system for catching rain. Channels cut into the rock plateau fed rock-cut cisterns; one large rock-cut pit, possibly a cistern, is about 8 m across and 2.8 m deep. On a dry limestone hill with no spring, water storage suggests people stayed for long periods, perhaps year round. Domestic buildings: round to oval in the earliest phase, rectangular later (Clare 2020). Rainwater harvesting: rock-cut channels and cisterns on the plateau. Food processing: thousands of grinding tools, often on roofs and terraces (Dietrich L. et al. 2019). Fresh from the field (August 2026): geophysical survey reported by Karul's team detected several large buildings near the enclosures whose layouts suggest dwellings. None of this makes the enclosures ordinary. They still look like special buildings, used for gatherings and rituals. But the picture has shifted from a lonely temple visited by nomads to a settlement with monumental communal buildings at its heart. That shift matters for the big story of the Neolithic, because it means that settling down, building big and experimenting with farming happened together, feeding one another.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 09 The comet on the Vulture Stone
chunks.text: In 2017 the chemical engineer Martin Sweatman and Dimitrios Tsikritsis proposed a bold reading of Pillar 43. Matching the animals to star patterns, they argued that the vulture, scorpion and other creatures form a sky map, and that the circle by the vulture's wing marks the Sun at a particular solstice. Their result: a date stamp of 10,950 BCE, give or take 250 years, which they linked to a proposed comet impact at the start of the Younger Dryas cold period. The headless man, they suggested, symbolises catastrophe and death. The excavation team replied the same year in the same journal, and further critiques followed. The main problems are easy to state. First, the proposed date is roughly 700 to 1,000 years older than the oldest radiocarbon dates for Enclosure D, so the pillar would record an event that happened centuries before the building existed. Second, matching animals to constellations is very flexible: with more than 60 carved pillars to choose from, and freedom to decide which animal is which star group, patterns can be found almost anywhere. Third, the scene ignores parts of the pillar, such as the headless figure's phallus, that fit poorly with a message of death. The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis itself remains contested among earth scientists, which is a separate debate. But the specific claim that Pillar 43 records a comet strike has not persuaded the archaeologists who work at the site or the wider field. Sweatman has kept developing the astronomical reading, most recently in a 2024 paper extending it to Karahan Tepe, so the debate is alive in print. Still, it remains an interpretation with a clear problem of dates, not an established finding. The proposed comet date sits centuries before the oldest dates for the building that carries it.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: 10 What we still don't know
chunks.text: Göbekli Tepe no longer needs to be a mystery to be astonishing. We know roughly when it was built, from what stone, with what tools, and what its builders ate. The unknowns are the deep ones. What did the stone figures represent: gods, ancestors, founding heroes? Why foxes, and why so many dangerous animals? How were work parties organised without chiefs that we can see in burials or houses? Were the enclosures roofed? And how many more lie under the mound and under the other Stone Hills? Roughly nine tenths of the mound has not been excavated, and the Taş Tepeler project is only a few years old. The next surprises will probably come from the ordinary layers, the houses, hearths and rubbish, which tell us how people lived around their stone giants.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: debate
chunks.text: Does Pillar 43 record a comet impact around 10,950 BCE? Yes: the carvings are a star map with a date. Sweatman and Tsikritsis (2017) match the animals to constellations and read the scene as the sky at a solstice around 10,950 BCE, linked to a proposed Younger Dryas comet impact. No: dates and method do not support it. The proposed date is 700–1,000 years older than the oldest radiocarbon dates for Enclosure D; animal-to-constellation matching is highly flexible; and the reading ignores parts of the pillar (Notroff et al. 2017). The bold claim: Pillar 43 is a record of a comet strike at the start of the Younger Dryas. Receipt Meter No receipts yet Busted Rock solid The idea is specific and testable, which is to its credit, but it fails the most basic test: the carving would predate the building that carries it by centuries. Pattern matching between carved animals and star groups allows many possible fits, and no independent evidence at the site points to an impact. Unless older dates for Enclosure D emerge, the comet reading has no receipts.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: debate
chunks.text: Were the enclosures deliberately buried? Yes: a ritual backfilling. Schmidt saw uniform rubble fill with bones and tools as intentional burial at the end of use. At Karahan Tepe, fill in stages capped by large slabs looks deliberate (Karul 2021). Mostly no: slope slides and gradual infill. Clare (2020) and Kinzel and Clare (2020) describe mixed older and younger debris that slid in from higher ground, with repairs during use, and inverse stratigraphy in radiocarbon samples. The bold claim: Göbekli Tepe's enclosures were intentionally buried in a single ritual act. Receipt Meter Hot debate Busted Rock solid The current excavation team favours natural slope slides plus gradual filling for Göbekli Tepe itself, and the mixed dates support that. Yet intentional filling is well attested at Karahan Tepe and at other Neolithic sites, so some deliberate closing of buildings cannot be ruled out. The single-burial version looks weaker than it did in the 2000s.

chunks.heading: Göbekli Tepe: debate
chunks.text: Did people live at Göbekli Tepe, or only gather there? A sanctuary only. Schmidt's original model: no houses, a ceremonial centre visited by hunter-gatherer groups for feasts and building work. A settlement with monumental buildings. Domestic buildings, rock-cut cisterns, thousands of grinding tools and 2026 geophysical hints of large dwellings (Clare 2020; Dietrich L. et al. 2019). The bold claim: People lived at Göbekli Tepe for long periods, not only visited it. Receipt Meter Plausible Busted Rock solid Houses, water storage and bulk food processing are hard to explain for a site used only for brief gatherings. What remains unclear is how many people lived there, for how much of the year, and whether the enclosures and houses were in use at exactly the same time.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge
chunks.text: Salisbury Plain, England Stonehenge 11 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read c. 700 km distance travelled by the Altar Stone from northeast Scotland Clarke et al. 2024 c. 230 km from the Preseli bluestone quarries in Wales Parker Pearson et al. 2019 c. 25 km from West Woods, source of most sarsens Nash et al. 2020 50 of 52 sarsens chemically matched to one source Nash et al. 2020 c. 1,500 years of building and rebuilding Darvill et al. 2012 56 holes in the ring of Aubrey Holes Darvill et al. 2012 c. 3000–1500 BCE, in five main stages In use 30 uprights, c. 4.1 m high, c. 33 m across Sarsen circle trilithon uprights up to c. 7 m above ground; sarsens typically c. 25 t Largest stones West Woods, c. 25 km north (50 of 52 tested) Sarsen source Preseli Hills, Wales, c. 230 km Bluestone source c. 6 t sandstone from northeast Scotland, c. 700 km Altar Stone midsummer sunrise to midwinter sunset Axis Stonehenge grew in stages over about 1,500 years. A circular ditch and bank came first around 3000 BCE, with a ring of 56 pits, the Aubrey Holes. Around 2500 BCE the great sarsen circle and five trilithons were raised, and the smaller Welsh bluestones were set up and later rearranged several times. Geochemistry has matched most sarsens to West Woods, about 25 km north, and bluestones to outcrops in the Preseli Hills of Wales. In 2024 mineral dating showed the 6-tonne Altar Stone came from northeast Scotland. The stones were shaped with stone hammers, raised with levers, ropes and timber, and locked together with joints borrowed from carpentry. The myth The stones are too heavy and far-travelled for Neolithic farmers, so Merlin brought them by magic from Ireland, or glaciers dumped them conveniently nearby. The reality Quarries with stone wedges and hearths have been ex

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 01 Sunrise on the longest day
chunks.text: Stand in the middle of Stonehenge before dawn on the summer solstice and look northeast, out through the gap in the great ring. The sun comes up close to the Heel Stone, a lone sarsen outside the circle, and its first light runs straight down the monument's axis to the centre. Turn around and you face the opposite direction, where the sun sets at midwinter. The whole design is threaded on that one line. That alignment is one of the few things about Stonehenge nobody seriously disputes. Almost everything else, who built it, how, from what, and why, has been argued over for centuries. What has changed in the last decade is the quality of the receipts. Chemistry, mineral dating, isotopes in teeth and radiocarbon have turned a romantic ruin into one of the best-documented prehistoric monuments in the world, and the story they tell is more remarkable than the legends. Since 1986 Stonehenge and the nearby circles of Avebury have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, part of a landscape packed with hundreds of burial mounds, earthworks and ritual monuments. Understanding the stones means reading that whole landscape, and some of the most important evidence of the last twenty years has come from outside the circle. Stonehenge was not built once. It was built, rebuilt and rearranged for about fifteen centuries, like a cathedral that never stopped being renovated.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 02 Fifteen centuries of rebuilding
chunks.text: The standard framework, published by Timothy Darvill, Peter Marshall, Mike Parker Pearson and Geoff Wainwright in 2012, divides the site into five stages. Around 3000 BCE, people dug a circular ditch about 110 m across, piled the chalk into a bank inside it, and dug a ring of 56 pits now called the Aubrey Holes after the 17th-century antiquary John Aubrey. Cremated remains of many people were buried in and around them, making early Stonehenge one of the largest cemeteries of its time in Britain. Two plans. Left: the site plan with north up, showing the circular ditch and bank about 110 m across with entrances to the northeast and south, the ring of 56 Aubrey Holes, four Station Stones on a rectangle, dotted rings of Y and Z Holes, the stone circle in the centre, the Heel Stone outside the northeast entrance, and the Avenue running northeast. A line through the centre marks the solstice axis, midsummer sunrise to the northeast and midwinter sunset to the southwest. A 50 m scale bar. Right: an enlarged plan of the stones with a 10 m scale bar, showing the ring of 30 sarsen uprights about 33 m across, the bluestone circle inside it, the horseshoe of five trilithons open to the northeast, the inner bluestone horseshoe, and the Altar Stone lying across the axis. A key colours the five building stages. The Aubrey Holes may have held more than bones. When one of them, Aubrey Hole 7, was re-excavated in 2008, the chalk at its base was crushed as if by the weight of a standing stone. Many archaeologists now think the first bluestones stood in this outer ring around 3000 BCE, five centuries before they were moved into the centre. If so, the Welsh stones were there from the very beginning, and the monument started life as a stone circle and cemetery together. Around 2500 BCE came

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 03 The sarsens: a 25 km drag
chunks.text: The big stones are sarsen, a very hard silcrete that forms in blocks across southern England. For a long time the Marlborough Downs, about 25 to 30 km north, were assumed to be the source, but nobody could test it. The breakthrough came from an unlikely place. During restoration in 1958, a core was drilled through Stone 58, one of the trilithon uprights, and one of the workers kept it. In 2019, Robert Phillips returned it for study. In 2020 a team led by geomorphologist David Nash published the results in Science Advances. Using portable X-ray fluorescence, they showed that 50 of the 52 surviving sarsens share a common chemistry. Analysis of the core matched it to sarsen at West Woods, about 25 km north of Stonehenge. Two stones differ and came from somewhere else, still unknown. The core itself was a small revelation. Sarsen turns out to be almost pure quartz: sand grains cemented together by more quartz, which makes it one of the hardest and most durable building stones in Britain. That explains both why the stones have survived four and a half thousand years of weather and why shaping them was such hard work. Every flat face and curve was produced by pounding with hand-held mauls of the same material. The sarsens were not simply found and dropped into place. They were dressed with hammerstones, sometimes to remarkably fine finishes, and shaped with subtle refinements: the uprights taper, and the lintels are curved in plan so that together they form a true circle. A sarsen upright of the outer circle weighs about 25 tonnes; the largest trilithon stones are heavier. Moving them 25 km over the rolling chalk probably meant sledges on timber rails, ropes and large, well-fed teams.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 04 The bluestones: from Wales, on purpose
chunks.text: The smaller stones, about 80 originally of which 43 survive, are a mixed family of volcanic and igneous rocks called bluestones, and they are not local at all. Since the 1920s geologists have traced them to the Preseli Hills in southwest Wales, about 230 km away. Since 2011 excavations by Parker Pearson and colleagues have found the actual quarries: Carn Goedog, source of the spotted dolerite, and Craig Rhos-y-felin, source of a distinctive rhyolite. At both outcrops the rock forms natural pillars. The quarry workers left stone wedges driven into the joints, hearths, and artificial stone platforms at the foot of the outcrop where a freed pillar could be lowered onto a sledge.
