Radiocarbon dates from the quarries cluster around 3400 to 3000 BCE, around the time of Stonehenge's first stage. Typical pillars were about 4 m long and weighed around 2 tonnes. Why go so far? One answer comes from the dead. Isotope analysis of cremated bone from the first stage, published in 2018, found that about 10 of 25 individuals had not lived locally in the last years of their lives, and their values are consistent with west Wales. Stonehenge seems to have been, from the beginning, a meeting place of distant communities, and the stones may have carried ancestral meaning from home. In 2025 a team led by Jane Evans and Mike Parker Pearson analysed a cow's tooth buried at Stonehenge's south entrance around 3000 BCE. Lead and other isotopes show the animal spent part of its life on older Palaeozoic rocks like those of Wales, suggesting cattle, and perhaps cattle pulling sledges, came east with the bluestones.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 05 The Altar Stone: 700 km from Scotland
chunks.text: At the centre of the monument lies a fallen slab of greenish sandstone about 4.9 m long and weighing about 6 tonnes, partly buried under two collapsed sarsens. Since the 1920s it had been assumed to come from Wales, like the bluestones. In 2024, a team led by Anthony Clarke of Curtin University dated tiny zircon, apatite and rutile grains inside fragments of it. Their ages matched the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland, not Wales. The distance is about 700 km in a straight line and at least 750 km by any realistic route, over mountains and rivers, or around the coast by sea. A follow-up study in 2024 ruled out Mainland Orkney itself, pointing to the Scottish mainland. In 2026, Clarke's team tested whether ice could have done the work. Their modelling suggests Ice Age glaciers might have carried it part of the way, perhaps as far as Dogger Bank in what is now the North Sea, but that no ice route reached southern England, so people still had to move it hundreds of kilometres, probably in stages combining overland hauling with river or coastal transport. A six-tonne slab from the far north of Britain lies at the heart of a monument on the south coast plains. That is a statement about connections, not just muscle. How would you move it? No Neolithic boat big enough has been found in Britain, but the absence of evidence is not surprising, since plank or hide boats rarely survive. By land, a sledge on timber rails over some 750 km of hills, bogs and rivers would have taken many months and a relay of communities along the way. Either route implies alliances stretching the length of the island, and a reason strong enough to make the effort worthwhile. It also rewrites our picture of Neolithic Britain. Communities in Orkney, Wales and Wessex shared pot

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 06 Raising a trilithon
chunks.text: No Neolithic engineer left instructions, but excavated stoneholes preserve some of the method. Several have one sloping side, a ramp down which the base of a stone could slide, and a steep opposite face where it would come to rest. Once the stone had tipped into the hole, teams hauling on ropes, perhaps over a timber frame, pulled it upright, and the hole was packed with rammed chalk and broken stone. Step 1 of 5. A sarsen arrives on timber rails beside a pit with one sloping side and stakes along its steep back. A sarsen arrives on timber rails beside a pit with one sloping side and stakes along its steep back. Levered forward, the stone tips and slides base-first down the slope into the pit. Teams haul it upright with ropes, perhaps over a timber frame, and pack the pit with stones and rammed chalk. The lintel is raised, perhaps on a timber crib built up layer by layer, perhaps up an earth ramp. The lintel's mortises drop over the uprights' tenons; neighbouring lintels lock with tongue-and-groove joints. Five-step cutaway drawn at one scale beside a 1.7 m person, with chalk below ground. Step 1: a sarsen about 5.4 m long lying on timber rails beside a pit with a sloping side and timber stakes at its steep back. Step 2: levered forward, the stone tips and slides base-first down the slope into the pit. Step 3: the stone stands upright against the stakes, hauled by ropes over a timber A-frame, with packing stones in the pit. Step 4: two uprights about 4.1 m high with two tenons each; a lintel rests on a crib of crossed logs beside them and is levered across. Step 5: the lintel sits on the uprights, its mortises over the tenons, with an inset showing mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints. Lintels posed the harder problem: lifting a stone of about 7 tonnes more th

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 07 Durrington Walls and the living
chunks.text: Stonehenge was not an isolated temple on an empty plain. About 3 km to the northeast lies Durrington Walls, a huge henge enclosure. Excavations between 2004 and 2007 found the remains of houses dating to around 2500 BCE, the time the sarsens went up, and enormous quantities of animal bone and pottery. The pig bones are especially telling. Most pigs were killed at around nine months old, which, given spring births, puts the feasts in midwinter. Isotope studies published in 2019 show that pigs and cattle were brought to the feasts from across Britain, some probably from as far as Scotland. Parker Pearson has argued that Durrington, with its timber circles, was a place for the living and Stonehenge, in stone, a place for the ancestors, the two linked by the River Avon and their avenues. That interpretation is influential but not universally accepted. Where the Avenue meets the River Avon, excavators in 2009 found the stoneholes of a small circle of about 25 stones, nicknamed Bluestonehenge. Its stones seem to have been removed around 2400 BCE, perhaps taken up the Avenue and added to Stonehenge itself. Monuments in this landscape were not fixed: they were dismantled, moved and combined, as if the stones themselves carried histories worth keeping. The wider landscape keeps producing surprises. In 2020, geophysical survey revealed a ring of large pits, more than 20 of them, surrounding Durrington Walls on a circle about 2 km across, dug around 2500 BCE. Their purpose is unknown.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 08 Magic, glaciers and computers
chunks.text: In the 1130s the chronicler Geoffrey of Monmouth told how the wizard Merlin brought a stone circle called the Giants' Dance from Ireland by his arts. Oddly, the legend of stones moved from the far west to Salisbury Plain has a grain of truth in it; only the magic and the Irish address are wrong. The Druids arrived in the story much later. In the 17th and 18th centuries John Aubrey and William Stukeley linked Stonehenge to the Druid priests described by Julius Caesar, and the connection stuck. But the Druids belong to the Iron Age, roughly 2,000 years after the sarsens were raised. Modern Druid and pagan groups who gather at the stones for the solstice are part of the monument's long afterlife, not its origin, and English Heritage now opens the site to them on the longest and shortest days. A more serious rival to human transport is ice. Some geologists have argued since the 1970s that glaciers carried the bluestones most of the way to Salisbury Plain. The evidence has turned against this: there are no scattered Welsh erratics across Wiltshire, the quarries at Carn Goedog and Craig Rhos-y-felin show human extraction, and the Altar Stone modelling rules out a glacial route from Scotland. In 1965 the astronomer Gerald Hawkins proposed in Stonehenge Decoded that the monument was an astronomical computer, with the Aubrey Holes used to predict eclipses. Archaeologists, notably Richard Atkinson in a paper he titled 'Moonshine on Stonehenge', pointed out that the features Hawkins used belonged to different centuries and that many alignments occur by chance in any complex site. The solstice axis is real and deliberate; a Neolithic eclipse calculator is not supported.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: 09 What is still unknown
chunks.text: The exact routes of the bluestones and the Altar Stone, and whether boats were used for part of either journey. Whether the bluestones stood first in a circle in Wales. Excavations at Waun Mawn, published in 2021, were presented as a dismantled 'original Stonehenge', but that reading has been strongly challenged. Whether the sarsen circle was ever complete. Parchmarks seen in the dry summer of 2013 suggest missing stones once stood, but not every hole has been dated. Where the two non-West Woods sarsens came from. What the monument meant: a temple of the sun, a monument to the ancestors, a place of healing, or several of these at different times. The mystery rating is 2 out of 5. The how is increasingly well understood and the where is now known in startling detail. The why, as with most prehistoric monuments, may never be fully recoverable. But the builders' choices, a line to the solstice sun, stones hauled from three corners of Britain, joints copied from carpentry, tell us they were organised, ambitious and deeply connected to one another.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: debate
chunks.text: Did glaciers or people bring the far-travelled stones? Glaciers: ice sheets carried the bluestones, and perhaps the Altar Stone, much of the way. Britain was glaciated repeatedly; some geologists (e.g. Kellaway, Brian John) argue the Preseli quarries are natural features. People: the stones were deliberately quarried and hauled. Excavated quarries with wedges, platforms and dated hearths; no trail of Welsh erratics across southern England; 2026 ice modelling finds no glacial route for the Altar Stone into southern England. The bold claim: Ice, not people, delivered the Welsh bluestones and the Scottish Altar Stone to Salisbury Plain. Receipt Meter No receipts yet Busted Rock solid The glacial hypothesis was reasonable before the quarries were found. It now faces human-made quarry features dated to the right period, the absence of erratics where the ice would have dropped them, and modelling showing no glacier could carry the Altar Stone south from Scotland. Human transport is the far stronger explanation.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: debate
chunks.text: Was Stonehenge an astronomical computer? Yes: many alignments, and the 56 Aubrey Holes could track eclipse cycles. Gerald Hawkins, Stonehenge Decoded (1965); Fred Hoyle's later eclipse model. Only partly: the solstice axis is deliberate; the rest is over-reading. The features used date to different centuries; chance alignments are common in complex sites; the Aubrey Holes held cremations and possibly stones. The bold claim: Stonehenge was a Neolithic computer for predicting eclipses. Receipt Meter No receipts yet Busted Rock solid The midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset axis is solid and was built into every stage. But the eclipse-computer idea combines features that never existed together and relies on alignments that could arise by chance. Nothing in the excavated evidence requires or supports it.

chunks.heading: Stonehenge: debate
chunks.text: Was there an 'original Stonehenge' in Wales? Yes: the bluestones first stood in a circle at Waun Mawn in Preseli before being moved. Parker Pearson et al. 2021 reported empty stoneholes in an arc about 110 m across, the same diameter as Stonehenge's enclosure. Not shown: Waun Mawn was a smaller, incomplete arrangement unrelated to Stonehenge. Later critiques question the dating, the reconstructed diameter and whether some holes are stoneholes at all. The bold claim: The bluestones stood as a complete stone circle at Waun Mawn before being moved to Stonehenge. Receipt Meter Hot debate Busted Rock solid The Waun Mawn excavations found real stoneholes in the right region, and the idea fits the Welsh links shown by cremations and the cow tooth. But the dating is loose, the circle is incomplete, and specialists disagree strongly about the reconstruction. It remains an interesting hypothesis.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism
chunks.text: Antikythera shipwreck, Greece The Antikythera Mechanism 10 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read 82 fragments surviving pieces in Athens National Archaeological Museum, Athens 30 gears surviving bronze gearwheels Freeth et al. 2006 223 teeth on the main wheel b1 and on the Saros turntable e3 Freeth et al. 2006 c. 1.6 mm average spacing of the hand-cut teeth Freeth et al. 2006 69 gears in the 2021 reconstruction of the whole machine Freeth et al. 2021 c. 354 holes most likely count in the calendar ring Woan & Bayley 2024 82 Surviving fragments 30, hand-cut bronze with triangular teeth Surviving gears c. 13 cm across, 223 teeth Largest gear (b1) c. 34 × 18 × 9 cm (reconstruction) Case Metonic (19 yr), Saros (18 yr), Callippic, Exeligmos, Games Back dials most likely 354 holes, a lunar year (2020–2024 studies) Calendar hole ring c. 70–60 BCE, about 45 m deep Shipwreck A craftsman cut some 30 or more bronze gears by hand, with small triangular teeth about 1.6 mm apart, and mounted them in a wooden case with dials front and back. Turning a crank on the side drove the big main wheel, b1, once round for each year. Trains of gears with carefully chosen tooth counts turned that year into the motion of the Moon around the zodiac, the phase of the Moon, 19-year and 18-year calendar and eclipse cycles, and the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games. A pin-and-slot pair of gears reproduced the Moon's changing speed, following a theory of Hipparchos. X-ray computed tomography in 2005 revealed hidden tooth counts and thousands of letters of inscribed instructions. The myth Nothing like it existed for more than a thousand years, so it must be out-of-place technology, from time travellers, aliens or a vanished super-civilisation. The reality It fits a documented Greek tra

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 01 A lump of bronze from the sea
chunks.text: In 1900 a boat of sponge divers from the island of Symi, blown off course by a storm, took shelter at Antikythera, a small island between the Peloponnese and Crete. One diver, Elias Stadiatis, went down about 45 m and came back, in the story told ever since, babbling about a heap of dead naked people on the seabed. They were bronze and marble statues. The captain, Dimitrios Kontos, reported the find, and in 1900 and 1901 the divers, supported by the Greek navy, raised statues, glass, pottery and coins in one of the first large underwater excavations in history. Among the finds was a corroded lump of bronze and wood, not much bigger than a shoebox. It split into pieces as it dried. In May 1902, the archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed a gearwheel in one of them. A gearwheel, from a ship that coins and pottery date to around 70 to 60 BCE. The ship itself was a large merchant vessel carrying luxury goods from the Greek east, probably towards Italy, where wealthy Romans collected Greek art. Its cargo included bronze and marble statues, fine glassware, jewellery and pottery. The Mechanism may have been part of that cargo, or a possession of someone on board. Either way, it was already old and perhaps already repaired when the ship went down, which helps explain why dating its making is so difficult. A gearwheel, from a ship that sank more than two thousand years ago. It took a century to understand what it was for.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 02 Seventy years of squinting
chunks.text: The fragments were too fragile to take apart and too corroded to read easily. Early scholars, including the philologist Albert Rehm, guessed that it was an astronomical calculator, but the details were out of reach. The first person to make real progress was the historian of science Derek de Solla Price. From 1951 he studied the fragments, and in 1971 he worked with the Greek radiologist Charalampos Karakalos to make X-ray and gamma-ray images. His 1974 monograph, Gears from the Greeks, counted teeth, proposed a gear train and argued that the device was a calendar computer. Price got many things right and some things wrong. In the 1990s and 2000s Michael Wright, then a curator at the Science Museum in London, working first with Allan Bromley, used linear tomography to see layers inside the fragments. Wright corrected parts of Price's scheme, identified the Moon-phase display and built a working model, completed in 2002, that included a speculative display of the planets. Each generation saw a little deeper into the corroded blocks.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 03 2005: seeing inside the stone
chunks.text: The breakthrough came from new machines. In 2005 the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, a collaboration of British and Greek scientists and the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, brought two instruments to the museum. A high-energy X-ray computed tomography scanner built by the company X-Tek produced 3D slices through every fragment. A reflectance imaging dome developed at Hewlett-Packard photographed the surfaces under light from many angles, making faint letters on the corroded plates legible. The results, published by Tony Freeth and colleagues in Nature in 2006, were spectacular. The team counted teeth on gears hidden deep inside the fragments, confirmed the purpose of the back dials, and doubled the amount of inscription that could be read. The text turned out to be a user's manual in Greek, naming the dials, the planets and the cycles. At least 30 gears survive, most in the largest fragment. The biggest, the four-spoked main wheel called b1, is about 13 cm across and carried 223 teeth, each a little triangle about 1.6 mm from the next, cut by hand.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 04 Turn the crank, move the Moon
chunks.text: Imagine holding the box. On its side is a crank. Turning it drives b1, and one full turn of b1 is one year: a pointer on the front moves the Sun once around the zodiac and a day-by-day calendar. From b1 a train of smaller gears speeds the motion up. The tooth counts tell the story: 64 teeth drive 38, then 48 drive 24, then 127 drive 32. Multiply it out and the result is 254 turns for every 19 turns of b1. That is the number of times the Moon goes around the zodiac in 19 years, a ratio the Babylonians knew well. Step 1 of 5. Turn the crank: it drives the great main wheel b1 (223 teeth). One full turn of b1 is one year, and the Sun pointer moves once round the zodiac. Turn the crank: it drives the great main wheel b1 (223 teeth). One full turn of b1 is one year, and the Sun pointer moves once round the zodiac. The speed-up train b2 → c → d → e2 multiplies the rate by 254/19, about 13.37: the Moon's laps of the zodiac per year. The Moon pointer now moves. On the back, the big turntable e3 (223 teeth) carries the gears k1 and k2 round once in about 8.88 years, following the slow turning of the Moon's orbit. Pin and slot: k1 and k2 sit on slightly offset axes, so k2 alternately gains and loses a little. The Moon pointer speeds up and slows down, as in Hipparchos's lunar theory. Moon phase: a differential compares Moon and Sun and turns a half-dark ball on the Moon pointer to show the phase. Step 1: a crank turns the large four-spoked main wheel b1, 223 teeth, once per year, and the Sun pointer moves on a zodiac dial. Step 2: gears b2, c, d and e2 appear, with tooth counts 64 to 38, 48 to 24 and 127 to 32, giving 254 over 19, about 13.37 turns a year, and a Moon pointer appears. Step 3: a large turntable e3 with 223 teeth carries gears k1 and k2 and turns once in about 8.88 y

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 05 The back of the box: calendars and eclipses
chunks.text: The back of the Mechanism carried two large spiral dials, one above the other. A pointer with a small follower tracked each spiral groove, stepping outwards turn by turn like the needle on a record. Two tall rectangles show the front and back faces of the case, about 34 by 18 centimetres, with a 10 centimetre scale bar. The front has inscribed plates above and below a round dial with a calendar ring, a zodiac ring and dashed planet rings, plus a Sun pointer and a Moon pointer with a half-dark ball; the main wheel is shown faintly behind. The back has an upper spiral of five turns divided into 235 cells with two small subsidiary dials inside, labelled Games and Callippic, and a lower spiral of four turns divided into 223 cells with dots for eclipse glyphs and an Exeligmos dial in the centre. Upper dial, Metonic: 235 lunar months in a five-turn spiral, equal to 19 years. It let the user keep a lunar calendar in step with the solar year. The month names on it are Corinthian, a clue to where the owner lived or the maker learned his trade. Inside it, the Games dial: a four-sector dial naming the Panhellenic games, including Olympia, Isthmia, Nemea and Pythia, plus smaller festivals such as the Naa and the Halieia (Freeth et al. 2008). Also inside the Metonic dial, a Callippic dial for the 76-year cycle, four Metonic cycles with one day removed. Lower dial, Saros: 223 lunar months in a four-turn spiral, about 18 years and 11 days. Glyphs in 51 of the cells predict 38 lunar and 27 solar eclipses, some with the hour and, in later readings of the inscriptions, even the expected colour. Inside it, the Exeligmos dial: three Saros cycles, 54 years and about a month, which brings eclipses back at nearly the same time of day. The eclipse predictions are Babylonian in origin, based on

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 06 A cosmos on the front
chunks.text: The front dial is the most damaged part and the most debated. The inscriptions clearly mention the planets, and one fragment includes a list of synodic events for Venus and Mercury. But no planetary gears survive. In 2021 Freeth and colleagues at University College London published a full reconstruction, the Model of the Cosmos. They propose concentric rings on the front, displaying the Moon, the lunar nodes, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, with little index letters marking events such as stationary points and greatest elongations. To drive the planets they needed accurate period relations that could be built from reasonably sized gears. The inscriptions contain the numbers 462 and 442, which the team identifies as periods for Venus and Saturn: 289 synodic cycles in 462 years for Venus and 427 in 442 years for Saturn, relations they argue could have been derived with ancient Greek methods. Their model has 69 gears in all, 34 of them in the lost planetary system in front of b1. It fits inside the case and accounts for surviving clues, such as features on the spokes of b1 and an unexplained gear in one fragment. Much of the front is reconstruction, and the drawing marks it that way with dashed rings. The inscriptions tell us what was displayed; the surviving holes and bearings constrain where gears could sit; and the period relations must match ancient astronomy. Within those limits there could be more than one solution, so the 2021 model is a strong, carefully argued proposal rather than a recovered original.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 07 Fresh from the field: counting holes
chunks.text: Beneath the movable calendar ring on the front lies a ring of small holes, into which pins held the ring in place. Only part of it survives. How many holes were there? The calendar ring is marked with Egyptian month names and 365 days, so many assumed 365 holes. In 2020 a team led by Chris Budiselic measured the surviving holes on CT scans and argued statistically for about 354, the length of a lunar year. In 2024 the Glasgow physicists Graham Woan and Joseph Bayley reanalysed the data with methods borrowed from gravitational-wave astronomy. Their best estimate is about 355, or 354 if holes near fractures are excluded; 360 is strongly disfavoured and 365 is implausible under their model. They also found the holes were placed with remarkable care: the radial scatter of their positions is only about 0.028 mm around a circle about 77 mm in radius. If the result holds, the Mechanism tracked a lunar calendar as well as the Egyptian solar one. Other recent work adds healthy caution. A 2025 preprint by Esteban Szigety and Gustavo Arenas simulated the effect of the irregular, hand-cut triangular teeth and suggested that, as found, the gear train would have tended to jam or produce errors. That does not mean the device failed; it means the surviving, distorted fragments may not show the original precision, and that the maker was working at the edge of what hand tools allowed. A peer-reviewed response will be worth watching.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 08 Out of place? Not really
chunks.text: Because nothing comparable survives from antiquity, the Mechanism is a favourite of the ancient-mystery shelf. The argument goes like this: gearing of this complexity did not appear again for more than a thousand years, so it must come from outside history. Let us test that. First, written sources describe such devices. Cicero, writing in the 1st century BCE, tells in On the Republic (1.21–22) how the general Marcellus brought home from captured Syracuse a bronze sphere made by Archimedes that showed the motions of the Sun, Moon and planets, and even eclipses. In On the Nature of the Gods (2.88) he mentions a similar sphere made by his teacher Posidonius on Rhodes. Second, the Mechanism is written in Greek, uses Greek astronomical terms, follows Hipparchos's lunar theory and uses Babylonian cycles known from cuneiform tablets. Third, its manufacture shows the marks of hand work: slightly irregular teeth, repairs and adjustments. Why don't more survive? Because bronze was valuable and routinely melted down for reuse. The Mechanism escaped only because it sank. Its uniqueness is a fact about survival, not about origin. The tradition did not vanish entirely either. A small geared sundial-calendar from the Byzantine world, about 1,500 years old and now in the Science Museum in London, shows that the idea of driving astronomical displays with gears survived in simpler forms. Medieval scholars in the Persian and Arabic-speaking world described geared calendars, and European astronomical clocks took the idea to new heights from the 14th century. The Antikythera Mechanism is the earliest and most complex known survivor of a long line, not an isolated miracle.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 09 Who made it, and when?
chunks.text: The Corinthian month names point to a place that used a Corinthian-style calendar, such as Corinth's colonies in northwest Greece or Syracuse in Sicily, the city of Archimedes. The Games dial includes the Naa, held at Dodona in Epirus, which supports a northwestern Greek connection for the user. Others have linked the astronomy to Rhodes, where Hipparchos worked and Posidonius later built his sphere. These ideas are not mutually exclusive: a device could be designed in one tradition and made or set for use in another. The date is also debated. Letter forms and the ship's cargo suggest the 2nd or early 1st century BCE. In 2014 Christián Carman and James Evans argued from the eclipse predictor that its cycle begins in 205 BCE. A 2022 study by Aristeidis Voulgaris and colleagues proposed a starting date in 178 BCE. Neither date tells us when it was built, only the moment its calendar was set to start.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: 10 What we still don't know
chunks.text: We know what most of it did. We do not know who made it, or for whom: a rich collector, a teacher, a temple? We do not know exactly how the planetary display worked, because those gears are lost. We do not know how accurate it was in use, or how many similar devices existed. And divers returning to the wreck since 2014 have found more objects, so small pieces of the story may still be lying on the seabed. There is also the question of accuracy. The Mechanism's cycles are excellent over years, but its Babylonian-style models were not perfect, and any hand-made gear train accumulates small errors. A user would probably reset it from time to time against the sky or a calendar, much as we still adjust clocks. Future scans with even higher resolution may tell us more about wear on the teeth, which would show how much it was actually used. What the Mechanism shows is simpler and more human: a Greek craftsman with files, saws and a head full of Babylonian and Greek astronomy built a pocket model of the sky, and it took twentieth- and twenty-first-century X-ray machines to read what he had written on it.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: debate
chunks.text: Is the Mechanism out-of-place technology? Yes: too advanced for its time. No comparable geared device survives from antiquity, and similar complexity reappears in European astronomical clocks only in the medieval period. No: it belongs to a Greek tradition. Cicero describes geared spheres by Archimedes and Posidonius; the inscriptions are Greek; the gearing follows Hipparchos's lunar theory and Babylonian cycles; hand-work marks and errors are visible. The bold claim: The Antikythera Mechanism could not have been made by ancient Greeks. Receipt Meter Busted Busted Rock solid Every part of the device is explained by known Greek and Babylonian astronomy and by hand tools of the period. Written sources describe similar instruments, and bronze recycling explains why so few survive. Its rarity is a survival accident, not evidence of an outside origin.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: debate
chunks.text: Did the front show all five known planets? Yes: a full cosmos. The inscriptions name the planets and list their synodic events; the 2021 model fits 34 planetary gears in front of b1 using ancient-style period relations (Freeth et al. 2021). Unproven: the gears are lost. No planetary gear survives; alternative layouts are possible, and the 2021 relations are reconstructed rather than read directly from surviving teeth. The bold claim: The Mechanism displayed the positions of Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. Receipt Meter Plausible Busted Rock solid The inscriptions make a planetary display very likely, and the 2021 model shows that it could fit. But without surviving planetary gears, the exact design remains a reconstruction.

chunks.heading: The Antikythera Mechanism: debate
chunks.text: Did the calendar ring count a 354-day lunar year? Yes: about 354 holes. Two statistical analyses of hole positions on CT scans favour c. 354–355 holes; 360 is strongly disfavoured and 365 implausible (Budiselic et al. 2020; Woan & Bayley 2024). Not certain. Only part of the ring survives, the fragments are distorted, and the visible calendar scale uses 365 Egyptian days. The bold claim: The hidden ring of holes under the calendar ring had about 354 holes. Receipt Meter Strong Busted Rock solid Independent analyses using different statistical methods converge on about 354. The result depends on assumptions about how regularly the holes were spaced, but the precision of the surviving holes supports those assumptions.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
chunks.text: Mediterranean and Mesopotamia The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World 10 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read 7 wonders on the canonical list Antipater of Sidon, Greek Anthology 9.58 1 standing still standing today, the oldest of them Clayton and Price 1988 56 years that the Colossus of Rhodes stood before an earthquake toppled it Pliny, Natural History 34.41 127 columns in the rebuilt Temple of Artemis at Ephesus Pliny, Natural History 36.95 over 3,300 pieces architectural fragments catalogued underwater at Alexandria Empereur and CEAlex surveys since 1994 0 texts known Babylonian texts that describe the Hanging Gardens Dalley 2013 1 of 7 (the Great Pyramid) Still standing about 2,300 years apart (c. 2560 to c. 280 BCE) Oldest to newest Great Pyramid, c. 146.6 m; Pharos c. 100 m or more Tallest Colossus of Rhodes, stood 56 years (Pliny) Shortest-lived 127 columns, each 60 Roman feet (c. 18 m), per Pliny Temple of Artemis none known Babylonian texts describing the Gardens The list itself was a Greek creation: a canon of theamata, 'things to be seen', not an official ranking, and its membership shifted before settling on the familiar seven. The wonders span 2,300 years and very different techniques: a mountain of cut limestone in Egypt, marble temples and tombs in western Anatolia, a gold and ivory statue at Olympia, a colossal bronze on Rhodes, and a stone tower with a fire at its summit at Alexandria. For the Hanging Gardens, Assyriologist Stephanie Dalley argues that the Greek accounts describe Sennacherib's palace garden at Nineveh, watered by canals and aqueducts, rather than a garden at Babylon. The myth The Colossus straddled the harbour of Rhodes, the Pharos had a mirror that burned enemy ships, and the Hanging Gardens were built by Nebuchadnezzar fo

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 01 A bucket list, written in verse
chunks.text: Some time around or before 100 BCE, a poet from Sidon named Antipater wrote a short epigram that reads like a travel boast. He had seen the great sights of his world, he says, and then he saw one more that outshone them all. His poem is one of the earliest surviving lists of what we now call the Seven Wonders. I have set eyes on the wall of lofty Babylon on which is a road for chariots, and the statue of Zeus by the Alpheus, and the hanging gardens, and the colossus of the Sun, and the huge labour of the high pyramids, and the vast tomb of Mausolus; but when I saw the house of Artemis that mounted to the clouds, those other marvels lost their brilliancy. Notice two things. First, Antipater's seven include the walls of Babylon, not the lighthouse of Alexandria; the list was not yet fixed. Second, he is not ranking engineering. He is describing theamata, 'things to be seen', the must-sees of a Greek-speaking traveller in the world opened up by Alexander's conquests. Silhouettes of the Seven Wonders standing on one ground line at the same scale, with guide lines at 50, 100 and 150 m. From left: the Great Pyramid, 146.6 m, partly cut off; the Hanging Gardens as dashed green terraces about 25 m high, labelled place unknown; the Temple of Artemis with columns about 18 m; the Statue of Zeus, about 12 m, seated inside a dashed temple outline; the Mausoleum, about 45 m; the Colossus of Rhodes, about 33 m, standing on land; and the Pharos, about 100 m or more. A 1.7 m person is a tiny mark between the Temple of Artemis and Zeus. Drawn together at one scale, the seven make an odd family. One is a geometric mountain. Two are temples or tombs, two are colossal statues, one is a tower and one is a garden nobody can find. Their ages span 2,300 years, so that the Great Pyramid was alre

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 02 Who chose the seven?
chunks.text: Nobody, exactly. Greek writers had compiled lists of marvels since at least the 3rd century BCE; the scholar-poet Callimachus is said to have written one, now lost. A short treatise On the Seven Wonders survives under the name of Philo of Byzantium, although scholars doubt it is by the famous engineer of that name and date it much later. Its list matches Antipater's, and the manuscript breaks off before the last entry. Seven was a satisfying, sacred-feeling number, and the choices reflect a Greek view of the world: six of the seven stood in lands ruled by Greek-speaking kings after Alexander, and the seventh was in Egypt, which Greeks had long admired. The Pharos only displaced the walls of Babylon in later lists, and the canonical modern seven became standard in the Renaissance, when artists such as Maarten van Heemskerck engraved them as a set. The Seven Wonders are less a verdict on ancient engineering than a snapshot of what Greek tourists thought worth the trip.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 03 The survivor: the Great Pyramid
chunks.text: The oldest wonder is the only one still standing. Built for Khufu around 2560 BCE, the Great Pyramid rose about 146.6 m on a base about 230 m square, the tallest human-made structure for roughly 3,800 years. We know unusually much about how it was built, from the quarries on the Giza plateau, the settlement of its workers, and even the logbook of a boatman named Merer who shipped its white casing stone. It has its own deep dive in this collection, so here it serves as the yardstick: every other wonder in the drawing above is measured against it.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 04 The garden nobody can find
chunks.text: The Hanging Gardens are the wonder that most resists evidence. The earliest known mention comes from Berossus, a Babylonian priest writing in Greek around 290 BCE, quoted centuries later by Josephus: Nebuchadnezzar II, he says, built a 'hanging paradise' for a wife from Media who missed her mountains. Later Greek and Roman writers describe terraces on vaulted galleries, deep soil for large trees, and machines lifting water from the river. The park extended four plethra on each side, and since the approach to the garden sloped like a hillside and the several parts of the structure rose from one another tier on tier, the appearance of the whole resembled that of a theatre. The trouble is Babylon itself. Nebuchadnezzar left many inscriptions about his building works, and none mentions a garden. Robert Koldewey, who excavated the city from 1899 to 1917, identified a vaulted building in the Southern Palace as the substructure of the Gardens. Tablets found there turned out to record oil rations for foreign captives, including Jehoiachin, king of Judah, which suggests storerooms rather than a garden. In 1994, and at book length in 2013, Stephanie Dalley of Oxford proposed a bold solution. The Gardens were real, she argues, but they stood at Nineveh, more than 400 km to the north, in the palace of the Assyrian king Sennacherib around 700 BCE. Sennacherib boasted of a garden that was a wonder for all peoples, fed by a canal system that included a stone aqueduct at Jerwan about 280 m long, and he describes casting great bronze devices to raise water, which Dalley reads as early water screws. A relief from Nineveh shows a garden planted on terraces and arches, fed by an aqueduct. Later Greek writers, she suggests, confused Assyrian Nineveh with Babylon. Critics answer that Greek s

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 05 Zeus at Olympia: a god too big for his house
chunks.text: Around 435 BCE the Athenian sculptor Pheidias made a seated Zeus for the god's temple at Olympia, the sanctuary of the Olympic Games. Its core was a wooden framework covered with ivory for the skin and gold for the robes. Modern estimates put it at about 12 m high, inside a temple only about 20 m tall. Ancient visitors found it overwhelming, and slightly too big. The artist is thought to have missed the proper symmetry, for he showed Zeus seated but almost touching the roof with his head, thus making the impression that if Zeus arose and stood erect he would unroof the temple. Keeping such a statue alive took maintenance. The traveller Pausanias, writing in the 2nd century CE, says the floor in front of it was paved with black stone and edged to hold a shallow pool of olive oil, which helped protect the ivory from the damp of the Olympian valley. He also records that the descendants of Pheidias held the hereditary job of cleaning the statue. A wonder, in other words, came with a staff. The statue is gone, but its workshop was found. German excavators in the 1950s uncovered a building at Olympia with the same dimensions as the temple's inner chamber, containing tools, fragments of ivory and glass, and clay moulds used to shape the golden drapery. A small black-glazed jug from the site is inscribed on its base 'I belong to Pheidias'. Few ancient artists can be tied to a workshop so directly. The end is less certain. The sanctuary declined after pagan festivals were banned in the late 4th century CE. One Byzantine tradition says the statue was taken to Constantinople and destroyed in a palace fire around 475 CE; another has it perishing with the temple at Olympia. Either way, nothing of it is known to survive.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 06 Artemis at Ephesus: the wonder that burned
chunks.text: Antipater's favourite was the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, on the coast of modern Turkey. The first great marble temple there was begun around 550 BCE with gifts from Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia. In 356 BCE a man named Herostratus set it on fire, by later accounts simply to make his name immortal. Ancient writers liked to add that it burned on the night Alexander the Great was born. The Ephesians rebuilt it on the same plan and even larger. Pliny the Elder gives its size as 425 by 225 Roman feet, with 127 columns each 60 feet high, 36 of them carved with figures at the base. That makes a building about 125 m long and columns about 18 m tall. Damaged by Gothic raiders in the 260s CE and later quarried, it vanished into a marsh. The English engineer John Turtle Wood searched for it for six years before finding its pavement in 1869, some 6 m below the surface. In 1904 and 1905 David Hogarth dug beneath the earliest levels and found a foundation deposit of small electrum coins, among the oldest coins in the world. Today a single column, reassembled from fragments, stands in a pond where storks nest.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 07 The tomb that named all tombs
chunks.text: Mausolus, a Persian-appointed ruler of Caria in southwest Anatolia, died in 353 BCE. His wife and sister Artemisia completed the tomb he had begun at his capital, Halicarnassus (modern Bodrum). Pliny says it was designed by the architects Satyros and Pytheos and decorated by four famous sculptors, Scopas, Bryaxis, Timotheus and Leochares, one on each side. It stood 140 Roman feet high by Pliny's account, about 41 m, and modern reconstructions range up to about 45 m: a tall podium, a ring of columns, a stepped pyramid roof and, on top, a four-horse chariot. It was grand enough to give its name to every monumental tomb since. Earthquakes had damaged it by the Middle Ages, and between the 1490s and 1520s the Knights of St John reused its stones and burned its marble for lime while building their Castle of St Peter in Bodrum. In 1856 and 1857 Charles Newton excavated the site and shipped surviving sculptures to the British Museum, including two colossal figures long nicknamed Mausolus and Artemisia.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 08 The Colossus did not straddle anything
chunks.text: In 305 BCE the city of Rhodes survived a year-long siege by Demetrius, nicknamed the Besieger. To give thanks to their sun god Helios, the Rhodians sold the siege machines he abandoned and commissioned the sculptor Chares of Lindos to make a colossal bronze statue. It took 12 years. This statue, fifty-six years after it was erected, was thrown down by an earthquake; but even as it lies, it excites our wonder and admiration. Few men can clasp the thumb in their arms, and its fingers are larger than most statues. Pliny gives its height as 70 cubits, about 33 m, a little shorter than the Statue of Liberty from heel to head. It fell in the earthquake of about 226 BCE, and according to Strabo an oracle warned the Rhodians not to raise it again. The pieces lay where they fell for roughly 800 years. A Byzantine chronicler says that in the 650s CE they were sold to a merchant who carried the bronze away on 900 camels. How do you build a bronze giant? Pliny noticed that the broken limbs of the fallen statue gaped open and that large stones could be seen inside, which he took to be ballast used to steady it. The treatise attributed to Philo describes the figure being raised in place, course by course, with a mound of earth heaped around it as it grew, so that the workers were always on the ground. In 1956 the metalwork specialist Herbert Maryon argued that the skin was more probably made of hammered bronze plates fixed to an iron framework than of huge cast sections. The details are reconstruction, but a stone-weighted core inside an iron and bronze shell is the most widely accepted picture. The famous image of the Colossus with one foot on each side of the harbour entrance comes from medieval travellers' tales and Renaissance engravings, not from ancient sources. It is also impo

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 09 The Pharos: a lighthouse that named all lighthouses
chunks.text: The youngest wonder rose on the island of Pharos at the entrance to Alexandria's harbour, completed around 280 BCE under the early Ptolemies. Pliny credits its design to Sostratus of Cnidus and says it cost 800 talents. It stood for over 1,500 years, long enough to be measured by Arab travellers. Al-Balawi, visiting in 1166, gave the base as about 30 m a side and described the octagonal and cylindrical stages above it. Step 1 of 5. Square base: a tower about 30 m a side, with an internal ramp, rooms and windows (al-Balawi, 1166). Square base: a tower about 30 m a side, with an internal ramp, rooms and windows (al-Balawi, 1166). Octagonal tier: a narrower eight-sided stage about 16 m across. Cylindrical top: a round lantern about 8.7 m in diameter. Fire and mirror: a fire burned at night; medieval writers also describe a mirror reflecting sunlight by day. Statue: Roman coins show a figure on the summit, probably Zeus or Poseidon. Total height c. 100 m or more. Elevation of the Pharos of Alexandria on a rocky base above the sea, with a 20 m scale bar and a 1.7 m person. Step 1: a tall square tier about 30 m wide with rows of windows. Step 2: an octagonal tier about 16 m across. Step 3: a cylindrical lantern about 8.7 m in diameter with openings. Step 4: a fire in the lantern, with a pale beam sweeping out over the sea. Step 5: a statue on the summit. A dimension line gives the total height as about 100 m or more. Why build it so tall? The Egyptian coast around Alexandria is low, flat and lined with shoals, and a sailor approaching from the open Mediterranean had almost nothing to steer by. A tower visible from far out at sea by day, and marked by a fire at night, turned a dangerous approach into a routine one for the grain ships that fed the Mediterranean world. It was a

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: 10 What remains uncertain
chunks.text: Where the Hanging Gardens were, if they were one real place: Babylon, Nineveh, or partly a literary composite. The exact pose and location of the Colossus of Rhodes. The Pharos's exact height and the true nature of its famous 'mirror'. The fate of Pheidias's Zeus after Olympia. The mystery rating for the set is 3 out of 5, and almost all of that comes from the Gardens. For the other six, the evidence ranges from very good (the pyramid, the Mausoleum sculptures, the Pharos blocks) to decent (the Colossus, known mainly from texts). Together they show what ancient builders prized: height, costly materials, famous artists, and above all the power to make a visitor stop and stare.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: debate
chunks.text: Were the Hanging Gardens really at Nineveh? Yes: the Greek accounts describe Sennacherib's garden at Nineveh. Sennacherib's inscriptions on his garden, canals, Jerwan aqueduct and bronze water-raising devices; a Nineveh relief of an irrigated terraced garden; the silence of Babylonian texts (Dalley 1994, 2013). No, or not shown: the Gardens were at Babylon, or largely literary. Every classical source names Babylon; Berossus was a Babylonian; no garden structure has been excavated at Nineveh; parts of Babylon remain unexcavated. The bold claim: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were actually Sennacherib's gardens at Nineveh. Receipt Meter Hot debate Busted Rock solid Dalley's case is careful and fits the Assyrian texts and images well, and it explains the Babylonian silence. But it relies on the Greek writers having confused two cities, and there is no excavated garden at Nineveh to confirm it. Leading specialists remain divided.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: debate
chunks.text: Did the Colossus straddle the harbour? Yes: it stood astride the harbour mouth, with ships sailing between its legs. Medieval travellers' stories and Renaissance engravings such as van Heemskerck's. No: it stood on land. No ancient source describes the pose; bronze legs spread across a harbour mouth could not carry the load; a fall would have blocked the harbour; ancient accounts describe the statue lying on the ground for centuries. The bold claim: The Colossus of Rhodes stood with one foot on each side of the harbour entrance. Receipt Meter Busted Busted Rock solid The image appears more than a thousand years after the statue fell. Ancient writers who saw its fallen pieces never mention a harbour pose, and the engineering of a 33 m bronze with its legs spread over open water does not work. Its exact site and pose are unknown, but a straddle is ruled out.

chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: debate
chunks.text: Could the Pharos's mirror burn ships? Yes: a great mirror focused sunlight to set enemy ships on fire. Medieval Arab and later European legends about the Pharos mirror. No: at most a polished surface to reflect daylight or firelight as a signal. No ancient source mentions the weapon; focusing enough sunlight to ignite a ship at sea from a tower would need an enormous, precisely curved mirror aimed at a moving target. The bold claim: The Pharos of Alexandria carried a mirror that burned enemy ships at sea. Receipt Meter No receipts yet Busted Rock solid The mirror is reported only in medieval accounts written long after the tower had been damaged, and the burning story belongs to the same legendary tradition as Archimedes' death ray. A reflector for signalling is plausible; a ship-burning weapon has no evidence behind it.

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: 01 The lumps everybody ignored
chunks.text: Pick up a fist-sized chunk of Roman concrete and you will see grey volcanic grit, dark nuggets of rock, perhaps a red sliver of broken tile. Look closer and you will also see white specks, some as small as a grain of rice, some the size of a pea. For more than a century, archaeologists and engineers glanced at these lime clasts and shrugged. They looked like the Roman equivalent of lumps in gravy: evidence that someone in a hurry had not stirred the mortar properly. That shrug turned out to be a mistake. In 2023 a team led by Admir Masic at MIT studied samples from a city wall at Privernum, south-east of Rome, and argued that the white lumps were not sloppiness but a signature. They were the leftovers of a particular way of making mortar, and they may be part of the reason so much Roman concrete is still standing. Two years later the same group walked onto a Roman building site at Pompeii that had been abandoned mid-job in 79 CE, and found the raw materials still sitting in piles. The white specks that looked like lazy mixing may be a built-in repair kit, waiting centuries for a crack. This is the story of a material that built harbours, aqueducts, markets and the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth. It is also a story about how much you can learn by taking old claims, and old lumps, seriously. Roman concrete is not magic, and it is not simply 'stronger' than ours. But it does things modern concrete struggles with, and chemists are only now working out how.

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: 02 Dust from Puteoli
chunks.text: The Romans did not invent lime mortar; builders around the Mediterranean had burned limestone for centuries. Heat limestone to around 900 °C and it gives off carbon dioxide and turns into quicklime, a caustic white powder. Add water and it becomes slaked lime, which slowly hardens again by soaking up carbon dioxide from the air. That is fine for plaster, but it sets slowly and never under water. The breakthrough came from the volcanic landscape around the Bay of Naples. Mix lime with the right volcanic ash and the ash's glassy, silica- and alumina-rich particles react with the lime to form a hard binder, even in wet conditions. The Romans called the best of it pulvis Puteolanus, the dust of Puteoli (modern Pozzuoli), and we still call such materials pozzolans. By the 2nd century BCE builders in Campania and Rome were using lime and ash mortars packed with chunks of tuff, the soft volcanic stone the region is made of. There is also a kind of powder which from natural causes produces astonishing results. ... This substance, when mixed with lime and rubble, not only lends strength to buildings of other kinds, but even when piers of it are constructed in the sea, they set hard under water. Vitruvius, writing in the 20s BCE, even gives a recipe for marine work: take the powder from the country between Cumae and the promontory of Minerva and mix it 'in the proportion of two to one', two parts ash to one of lime. A century later Pliny the Elder, who would die in the eruption of 79 CE, sounded almost indignant that such a humble material should be so powerful. Who could marvel enough, he asked, that the dust of the hills of Puteoli, once submerged, 'turns into a single mass of stone that withstands the attacks of the waves and becomes stronger every day' (Natural History 35.166

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: 03 Pouring stone into the sea
chunks.text: The boldest use of the new material was in harbours. Between 2002 and 2009 the Roman Maritime Concrete Study (ROMACONS), led by Christopher Brandon, Robert Hohlfelder, Marie Jackson and John Peter Oleson, drilled cores out of Roman piers, breakwaters and pilae (free-standing concrete blocks) at sites from Italy to Israel, Egypt, Crete and Turkey. They found blocks of remarkable size. Off Nisida in the Bay of Naples one pila has sides of up to 15.2 m and stands over 9.5 m tall. At Portus Iulius, the naval harbour Agrippa built in the 30s BCE, the outer pila measures about 10 by 10 m and more than 6 m high. Cross-section of a square concrete block, about 10 m wide, standing on the seabed in about 5 m of water. Timber posts driven into the seabed hold a lining of planks on both sides. Inside, seven horizontal bands of mortar packed with tuff chunks rise from the seabed; a dashed outline shows later layers reaching over 6 m. Seawater fills the rest of the form. A worker stands on a timber platform above; a rope from an A-frame lowers a basket of mortar into the water. Dimension lines and a 5 m scale bar give the size. How do you place concrete in the sea? Vitruvius describes driving a cofferdam of oak stakes with ties between them into the water, and the cores and timber impressions show several solutions in practice. In one common approach, the 'flooded form', a box of posts and planks was built on the seabed and the mortar was simply lowered into the seawater inside it, where it set without ever drying out. At Caesarea in Judaea, Herod's engineers went further, building double-walled wooden boxes about 11 by 15 by 4 m on shore, towing them out and sinking them, and casting barge-shaped forms full of concrete. One block from the North Breakwater measures roughly 15 by 11.5

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: 04 Crystals that grow out of seawater
chunks.text: Modern concrete does not love the sea. Salt water attacks the cement paste and, above all, the steel reinforcement inside it. Roman harbour concrete seems to have made peace with its environment instead, and Marie Jackson's team at the University of Utah has spent years working out why. In 2013 they reported aluminous tobermorite, a rare layered calcium silicate mineral, in the lime-rich parts of a breakwater from the Baianus Sinus in the Bay of Naples. Tobermorite is prized in engineering because its crystals are strong and platy, but making it synthetically usually requires high temperatures. In 2017, working on cores from the Baianus Sinus and Portus Neronis breakwaters and a pier at Portus Cosanus in Tuscany, they reported something stranger: tobermorite and a zeolite mineral called phillipsite had also grown later, at ordinary seawater temperatures, inside pores, in cracks and in the altered edges of volcanic crystals and pumice. Their interpretation is a slow, continuous reaction. Seawater percolates through the concrete, dissolves some of the volcanic glass and minerals, and the resulting alkaline fluids precipitate new, interlocking crystals. In other words, the sea that should be destroying the structure appears to be feeding it. Jackson's team has pointed out that this is what Pliny described: a mass of stone 'stronger every day'. He meant it as rhetoric, but the chemistry is now consistent with him. The sea that should be destroying the pier appears to be feeding it, one crystal at a time. It is important not to overstate this. The new minerals are observed in a handful of sampled structures, and 'growing crystals' is not the same as a measured increase in strength over centuries. The work does suggest, though, that the volcanic ash was not just a filler. It

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: 05 Hot mixing and the crack that heals itself
chunks.text: Back on dry land, the Privernum samples posed a different question: what are the white lime clasts? Vitruvius and Pliny both talk about lime that has been slaked (soaked in water) before use, and scholars long assumed Roman builders worked the same way. If you start with well-slaked lime paste, you should not get chunky white lumps. Linda Seymour, Admir Masic and colleagues mapped the clasts with electron microscopy and Raman spectroscopy and found textures that point to high temperatures. Their proposal, published in Science Advances in 2023, is 'hot mixing': quicklime, not only slaked lime, was mixed with the ash and aggregate, and then water was added. Quicklime reacts violently with water, heating the whole batch by roughly 55–60 °C and, locally, to more than 200 °C. That heat speeds up setting, allows chemical reactions that would not happen in a cold mix, and leaves behind brittle, porous nodules of calcium-rich material: the lime clasts. Step 1 of 5. A lime clast, left over from hot mixing, sits in the mortar: a porous, brittle lump of calcium-rich material. A lime clast, left over from hot mixing, sits in the mortar: a porous, brittle lump of calcium-rich material. A crack opens. Because the clast is weak, the crack tends to run through it, exposing fresh, reactive lime. Water seeps into the crack, as it would into any concrete. The water dissolves calcium from the clast and spreads a calcium-rich solution along the crack. The calcium recrystallises as calcium carbonate (or reacts with the volcanic ash) and seals the crack. In lab tests, cracks about 0.5 mm wide stopped leaking within weeks. A magnified block of grey-beige mortar studded with darker aggregate pieces and one large white lime clast. Step 1 highlights the clast. Step 2 adds a dark crack that runs f

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: 06 A building site frozen in 79 CE
chunks.text: Stand in a half-finished house at Pompeii in the summer of 79 CE. Walls are being rebuilt, perhaps after earthquake damage. Blocks of yellow tuff brought from the Naples area are stacked up, broken roof tiles have been set aside for recycling, and amphorae have been reused to hold lime. Then Vesuvius erupts and everything stops. That is roughly what archaeologists found at a house in Regio IX, insula 10, excavated in recent years. In a study published in Nature Communications in December 2025, E. Vaserman, James Weaver, Admir Masic and colleagues from MIT and the Pompeii Archaeological Park analysed the site's materials. Among them were piles of dry, premixed lime and volcanic ash, with fragments of quicklime several millimetres across, ready to be wetted and used. The team also recovered tools such as bronze and iron plumb bobs and balance scales, and found the site organised into separate storage areas for tiles, tuff and premixed mortar. The Pompeii study (Vaserman et al. 2025) gives the first direct archaeological snapshot of hot mixing in progress: dry lime and ash blended in advance, with quicklime fragments that match the lime clasts seen in finished Roman walls. It also shows that what a Roman architect wrote and what a Roman crew did were not necessarily the same thing. Vitruvius describes slaked lime; this crew was, it seems, working with quicklime. One site cannot tell us how every Roman builder worked for six centuries. What it does is turn hot mixing from an inference, based on textures under a microscope, into something you can see sitting on a building site. It also underlines a theme of this whole story: the most useful evidence is often in the mess, not in the manuals.

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: 07 Why your concrete cracks and theirs sometimes does not
chunks.text: In 1824 an English bricklayer, Joseph Aspdin, patented Portland cement, named for its resemblance to Portland stone. It is made by firing limestone and clay at around 1,450 °C into clinker, then grinding it with gypsum. Mixed with sand, gravel and water it forms concrete that is strong, fast and cheap, and when steel bars are cast inside to handle tension, you can build bridges and towers the Romans could only dream of. That same design creates the weak point. Steel rusts, and rust takes up more room than the steel it came from. Once water and salts reach the reinforcement, it expands, cracks the concrete from the inside and lets in more water. Jackson has put it bluntly: in the sea, much of our construction would be 'a mass of corroding steel' long before two thousand years had passed. Roman concrete, with no steel inside, never faced that problem. Strength: modern structural concrete is generally much stronger in compression than Roman mortars. Rome built massive walls because it had to. Durability: Roman mixes keep reacting with water; lime clasts can reseal cracks; there is no steel to corrode. Carbon: Portland clinker needs around 1,450 °C against roughly 900 °C for Roman lime, and cement production is responsible for about 8% of global CO₂ emissions (Lehne and Preston, Chatham House, 2018). Speed: Portland concrete sets and gains strength quickly and predictably, which modern construction schedules depend on. That is why engineers are interested. Nobody plans to build skyscrapers from tuff and lime, but Roman-inspired additives, such as volcanic ash replacing part of the Portland cement, or lime clasts added to encourage self-healing, could make some modern concretes last longer and emit less carbon. Several research groups are now testing such blends, including f

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: 08 Busting the super-concrete myth
chunks.text: Every few years a headline announces that scientists have 'finally cracked' the secret of Roman concrete, as if it were a lost formula locked in a vault. The reality is less mysterious and more interesting. The recipe was never lost: Vitruvius wrote it down, and ROMACONS mixed and cast it in the sea in 2004. What researchers have been uncovering is why particular mixes behave the way they do, and how Roman practice varied. There is also a survivor's bias. We see the Roman concrete that lasted: the Pantheon, harbour piers, aqueduct cores. We do not see the countless Roman structures that cracked, slumped or were quarried away. Some Roman builders cut corners, some local ashes were poor pozzolans, and plenty of Roman buildings needed repairs within decades. The surviving examples are a filtered sample of the best-built and best-placed. Open questions remain. How common was hot mixing across the empire, and did recipes differ between regions, periods and building types? How much of the durability of harbour concrete comes from the ash, how much from the lime, how much from the placement method? And can the slow, centuries-long reactions that help Roman concrete be sped up enough to be useful to engineers who cannot wait two thousand years for results? The recipe was never lost. What we are learning is why the best Roman mixes still work. What is not in doubt is the core lesson. The Romans built with materials that kept reacting with their surroundings, and they sometimes left in 'flaws' that turned out to be features. For a civilisation that produced some of history's great engineers, it is fitting that their humblest ingredient, a pinch of white lime in a grey mortar, is still teaching us something.

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: debate
chunks.text: Is Roman concrete simply better than modern concrete? Yes: it lasts far longer. Harbour structures have survived about 2,000 years in seawater, where modern reinforced concrete can degrade within decades. No: it is a different material with different strengths. Roman mortars are weaker in compression and slower to gain strength; their durability comes from reactive ash, lime clasts and the absence of corroding steel, plus survivor bias. The bold claim: Roman concrete is stronger than modern concrete. Receipt Meter Busted Busted Rock solid In raw strength, modern structural concrete generally wins by a wide margin. What the best Roman concretes have is longevity in particular settings, especially the sea, thanks to chemistry that keeps working and the lack of steel reinforcement. 'Better' depends on the job; 'stronger' is simply not what the evidence shows.

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: debate
chunks.text: Did Roman builders routinely hot-mix with quicklime? Yes: the clasts and the Pompeii site point that way. Lime clast textures at Privernum indicate high-temperature reactions, and the Pompeii building site had dry premixed lime and ash with quicklime fragments. Not yet shown to be universal. Vitruvius and Pliny describe slaked lime, and the direct evidence comes from a small number of sites and periods. The bold claim: Hot mixing with quicklime was a common Roman technique, not a one-off. Receipt Meter Plausible Busted Rock solid Two independent lines of evidence, microscopic textures and an actual building site, fit hot mixing, and lime clasts are common in Roman mortars. But sampling is still limited, and Roman practice varied across a huge empire and six centuries. The claim is well supported for some sites; its generality is still being tested.

chunks.heading: Roman concrete: debate
chunks.text: Is Roman concrete a lost secret? Yes: modern science cannot reproduce it. Popular articles regularly describe the recipe as lost or mysterious. No: the recipe survives and has been reproduced. Vitruvius records the mix; ROMACONS cast a Vitruvian pila at sea in 2004; labs have made hot-mixed, self-healing analogues. The bold claim: The Roman recipe is a lost secret that modern science cannot reproduce. Receipt Meter Busted Busted Rock solid The ingredients and proportions are documented in ancient texts and have been replicated. What is new is an understanding of the mechanisms, such as seawater-grown minerals and self-healing lime clasts. That is ordinary science filling in details, not the recovery of a lost formula.

Stepped rings outside add weight to the haunches, and 140 sunken coffers inside remove it where it is least useful. chunks.heading: The Pantheon dome: 01 A hole in the sky
chunks.text: Walk out of the bright, noisy Piazza della Rotonda, between granite columns as thick as tree trunks, through bronze doors taller than a two-storey house, and the city goes quiet. You are standing inside a sphere. The floor is a disc 43.3 m across; the dome above rises so that its top is exactly 43.3 m over your head. If you could inflate a giant ball in here, it would just touch the floor and kiss the roof. At the very top there is no roof at all. The oculus, a round opening about 8.3 to 8.9 m across depending on who measures it, is the building's only window. On a sunny day a disc of light, sharp-edged as a spotlight, crawls slowly across the coffers and down the walls. On a rainy day the rain falls straight in, and drains away through small holes in a floor that slopes gently to shed water. Nineteen centuries on, no one has built a larger unreinforced concrete dome. This is the Pantheon, rebuilt in the early 2nd century CE and in continuous use ever since, first as a temple and, from 609, as a church. It is probably the best-preserved major building of ancient Rome. How a structure this bold, made of concrete with no steel inside, has survived earthquakes, lightning, looting and nearly two thousand winters is a story of clever geometry, careful material choices and a couple of lucky breaks.

chunks.heading: The Pantheon dome: 02 Agrippa's name, Hadrian's building
chunks.text: Look up at the porch and the inscription seems to settle the question of authorship: M·AGRIPPA·L·F·COS·TERTIVM·FECIT, 'Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made this'. Agrippa, Augustus' right-hand man, did build a Pantheon here around 27 to 25 BCE. But that building burned in 80 CE, was restored under Domitian, and burned again after a lightning strike in 110. What stands today is a complete rebuild. For a long time it was credited to Hadrian, who became emperor in 117. Then archaeologists looked at the bricks. Roman brickyards often stamped their products with the names of owners, managers or consuls, which makes them datable. Lise Hetland's 2007 study and Mark Wilson Jones' later work showed that nearly all the stamps in the building are late Trajanic or early Hadrianic, pointing to construction starting around 114 CE, under Trajan, and finishing under Hadrian, with dedication around 125 to 128. At Rome he restored the Pantheon, the Voting-enclosure, the Basilica of Neptune, very many temples, the Forum of Augustus, the Baths of Agrippa, and dedicated all of them in the names of their original builders. So the inscription is a courtesy, not a lie: Hadrian, according to his ancient biographer, liked to put the original builders' names on the monuments he restored. It is also a neat reminder to read ancient labels with care. Who actually designed the new Pantheon is unknown. Hadrian was a keen amateur architect; Trajan's great engineer Apollodorus of Damascus has been suggested; the brick stamps make a Trajanic start likely, but no document names the architect.

chunks.heading: The Pantheon dome: 03 A sphere in a cylinder
chunks.text: The plan is disarmingly simple: a rectangular porch, a transitional block, and a round hall, the rotunda. The rotunda is a drum whose interior height to the springing of the dome equals the dome's radius, 21.65 m, so the hemisphere on top completes a perfect sphere. The drum wall is about 6.4 m thick, but it is not solid. It is carved into seven great niches plus the entrance bay, and threaded with hidden chambers and brick arches. Cross-section of the Pantheon rotunda drawn to scale. A thick cylindrical drum carries a hemispherical dome with an opening at the top. A dashed circle 43.3 m across fits exactly inside, touching the floor and the top of the dome. The walls and dome are shaded in six horizontal bands from dark to light, labelled travertine (foundation ring), travertine plus tuff, tuff plus brick, brick, brick plus light tuff, and light tuff plus pumice or scoria. Step rings climb the outside of the dome, coffers are cut into its inner surface, and dimension lines give 43.3 m for both diameter and height, c. 6.4 m for the drum wall and c. 8.3–8.9 m for the oculus. A tiny person stands on the floor for scale. From outside, the dome looks surprisingly low. That is because the drum wall rises well above the springing, to about 30 m, wrapping the heavy lower part of the dome. Above that, a series of stepped rings climbs the outside of the shell before it smooths into the gentle cap around the oculus. You see the sphere only from inside, which is precisely the point. The numbers are round in Roman terms. The diameter is usually equated with 150 Roman feet and the oculus with 30, and the portico columns were cut as 40-foot shafts. The building is a statement about geometry and the cosmos as much as about engineering. The ancient historian Cassius Dio, writing about

chunks.heading: The Pantheon dome: 04 Heavy at the bottom, light at the top
chunks.text: A dome is an arch spun around a vertical axis. Its weight pushes down, and near the base it also pushes outwards, trying to burst the ring it sits on. Unreinforced concrete handles squeezing very well but copes badly with being pulled apart. The Pantheon's designers attacked the problem from several directions at once, and the most elegant is the concrete itself. They graded the aggregate, the chunks of stone set into the mortar, by weight. In the foundation ring they used dense travertine. In the lower drum, travertine and tuff; higher up, tuff and broken brick; then brick; and in the upper dome, light tuff and volcanic scoria or pumice, some of it apparently brought from the Vesuvius region. Estimates of the concrete's density fall from about 1,600 kg per cubic metre at the dome's base to about 1,350 near the oculus. Modern normal concrete is around 2,400. It makes a big difference. In their 1986 structural study, Robert Mark and Paul Hutchinson found that if the dome had been built with heavy concrete throughout, the stresses in it would have been substantially higher, by their estimate some 80 percent. Instead, their model gives peak tensile stresses of only about 0.13 MPa, small enough for Roman concrete to tolerate in much of the structure. Nobody has sliced the Pantheon in half. The aggregate zones come from places where the concrete is exposed: damaged areas, openings in the upper drum, repairs, and observations made during restorations since the 19th century. They have been summarised by Mark and Hutchinson (1986), Lynne Lancaster (2005) and Mark Wilson Jones (2003, 2015). The exact heights of each zone are approximate, which is why diagrams, including ours, show them simplified. The shell thins as it rises, from about 6 m at its base to about 1.2 m at the ocul

chunks.heading: The Pantheon dome: 05 Cracks, rings and a keystone made of air
chunks.text: Here is a surprising fact: the Pantheon's dome is cracked, and has been for a very long time. Mark and Hutchinson showed that the lower part of the dome is under hoop tension, a stretching force around its circumference. Unreinforced concrete cannot hold much of that, so the dome cracked along its meridians, like the segments of an orange, probably soon after it was built. Wilson Jones has traced cracks in the rotunda up to about 7 cm wide. Step 1 of 7. Every part of the dome pushes down, and near its base a dome also tries to spread outwards. Unreinforced concrete resists squeezing well but cracks easily when pulled. Every part of the dome pushes down, and near its base a dome also tries to spread outwards. Unreinforced concrete resists squeezing well but cracks easily when pulled. The lower dome cracked along its meridians early on, so it now behaves partly like a ring of arches leaning on each other. Their thrust lines stay inside the concrete all the way down into the thick drum. The step rings add weight to the haunches, pushing the thrust down into the drum instead of outwards. Coffers and ever-lighter aggregate cut the weight where it matters most: near the crown, concrete of about 1,350 kg/m³ against about 1,600 at the base. Around the oculus, a ring of tiles set on edge is squeezed from all sides and works like a keystone for every arch at once. In the 6 m thick drum, brick relieving arches steer the loads around the niches into solid piers and down to the ring foundation. The oculus is the only window. Through the day a disc of sunlight crawls across the coffers and walls; around noon on 21 April it lights the entrance (Hannah & Magli 2011).
